48	## 4. Dataset and sample
49	- Source corpus and search:
50	  - [V] Search conducted in January 2026, covering all sources available up to January 2026 (p. 8).
51	  - [V] Final query: any of 13 TD-type terms (technical, code, design, documentation, infrastructure, architecture, test, defect, build, requirement, service, test automation, process debt) AND ("large language models" OR "AI-generated code" OR "LLMs" OR "LLM" OR "ChatGPT" OR "Copilot" OR "AI code" OR "AI assistance") (p. 9).
52	  - [V] The query was developed through exploratory refinement rounds; it was widened from "technical debt" only to all 13 Alves et al. types (p. 8–9).
53	- Grey literature:
54	  - [V] Google via SerpAPI, about 375,000 hits, limited to the first 10 result pages on the basis of relevance saturation (p. 9).
55	  - [V] After de-duplication and removal of academic papers: 132 unique sources (p. 9).

57	  - [V] Inclusion threshold: score above 11 of 22, giving 73 grey sources (p. 9). Mean score 14.4 (SD 2.52), 75th percentile 15.5 (p. 10).
58	  - [V] By tier (Table 3): tier 1 company blogs 38; tier 2 developer platforms 18 and media outlets 14; tier 3 personal blogs 3 (p. 10).

70	## 5. Experimental setup
71	- Procedure:
72	  - [V] Two authors independently applied data-extraction forms to all sources, and a third author resolved conflicts (p. 12).
73	  - [V] Extraction fields: TD types; LLM-unique TD concerns; mitigation strategies; tools; benchmarks or datasets; new metrics; notes (p. 12–13).
74	  - [V] For formal sources, Cohen's kappa was 0.93 for TD types and 0.90–1.00 for the other fields (p. 13).

[A] "Fast-integration debt" means rapidly integrating LLM output without validation; the authors link it explicitly to vibe coding ("developers implement AI suggestions quickly, or vibe code, without understanding their implications") and say it leads to governance debt (p. 17). 138	## 9. Limitations we identified
139	- [I] Frequency of mentions is not strength of evidence. Table 8 counts how many sources mention a debt type (p. 16), mostly from grey sources, and primary-study quality is not weighted. The headline new categories rest entirely on practitioner commentary: governance debt (19 grey, 0 formal) and fast-integration debt (13 grey, 0 formal) (p. 16). They are hypotheses, not established effects.
140	- [I] Fig. 4's y-axis reads "Number of Sources", but grey-source counts for 2025 (84 + 25 = 109) exceed the 73 grey sources (p. 19; values read from the Fig. 4 image, not in the text layer; re-checked 2026-11-12). The figure therefore counts mentions, not sources, which can inflate the visual trend.
141	- [I] No formal quality appraisal of the 31 peer-reviewed sources is described (p. 11–12), although the threats section claims one (p. 29). Weak primary studies (e.g. vision or position papers such as Mitchell et al.'s "Position: Vibe Coding Needs Vibe Reasoning", p. 21, p. 36) are counted like empirical studies.
142	- [I] Inclusion inconsistency: the review restricts formal sources to peer-reviewed work (p. 11), yet Della Porta et al. [157] is listed under EASE in Table 6 (p. 13) while its reference entry gives only an arXiv preprint (p. 36). PromptDebt also appears twice in the references, as a published version [14] and an arXiv version [15] (p. 31).
143	- [I] EC2 excludes papers on correctness or functional quality that do not frame findings as TD (p. 12). Empirical maintainability studies of LLM code that never use the term "debt" (for example SonarQube-based LLM vs human comparisons) may therefore be missing. molison2025llm (ESEM 2025, SonarQube effort-to-fix) does not appear in the reference list; we checked by text search of `fulltext.txt`. The authors partly acknowledge this term-based bias (p. 30).
144	- [I] The grey search covers only the first 10 Google result pages (p. 9), so results depend on Google's ranking at search time. The authors note that the ranking is undocumented (p. 30), and replication is likely to give different results.
145	- [I] Table 1 answers "No" to whether the formal literature lacks volume or quality of evidence (p. 7). This sits uneasily with the review's own conclusion that formal work is "small but growing" (p. 18) and lacks benchmarks and metrics (p. 24).
146	- [I] Grey quality scoring split the 132 sources between two authors with consensus afterwards, and no pre-reconciliation reliability was reported (p. 9). Kappa was computed only for formal-source extraction (p. 13).
147	- [I] The scope is LLM-assisted development in general, not application reconstruction or vibe-coded apps specifically. Vibe coding appears as a cause of fast-integration debt (p. 17, p. 26), and one formal source is a vibe-coding position paper (p. 21).

149	## 10. Threats to validity
150	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [A] Selection bias in screening and search-engine opacity are acknowledged (p. 30). [I] The keyword strategy is anchored on "debt"; with EC2 (p. 12) it selects sources that frame issues as debt, which may over-represent sources that already argue LLMs create debt.
151	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] English only; company blogs dominate (p. 30). [I] The corpus ends in January 2026 (p. 8); the field moves quickly (most sources are from 2025, p. 19).
152	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TD is operationalised as mentions of TD categories. Static-analysis indicators (SonarQube) are treated as "early signs" of TD (p. 22), which is itself an assumption. The review notes that TD tools disagree on what counts as real debt (p. 5).
153	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] Not applicable (no inferential statistics). Counts are descriptive and come from heterogeneous source types.
154	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Search string, databases, date, criteria, QA checklist and per-stage counts are reported (p. 8–12), and annotation sheets are on figshare (p. 4, p. 13). [I] The grey search is hard to reproduce (Google ranking, SerpAPI, first 10 pages). Per-source exclusion reasons at full-text stage are summarised but not itemised in the paper (p. 11).

1	# Research questions — Evaluating AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering for Software Application Reconstruction through Vibe Coding: Functional Fidelity, Code Quality, and Maintainability
2	
3	## RQ1: What AI/LLM approaches exist for reconstructing or generating software applications from observable artefacts (UI screenshots, designs, interaction behaviour, specifications), and how do they relate to vibe-coding workflows?
4	- Type: descriptive
5	- Why it matters: defines what "AI-assisted reverse engineering" currently looks like in practice and research, and which inputs and tools are realistic.
6	- Linked objective: O1
7	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
8	- Current answer: Six approach families exist (see reports/methodology-comparison.md §2):
9	  1. Screenshot or design to code [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @zhou2025declarui, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 6].
10	  2. Interaction video or before/after interaction screenshots to code [@chen2025iwr, p. 5; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
11	  3. Agentic rebuilds from a live running reference or an executable plus docs [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 3; @kim2026programdistill, p. 3; @yang2026programbench, p. 2].
12	  4. Natural-language spec or requirements to a full app [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 3; @lu2025webgen, p. 7; @tran2026vibe, p. 3; @pan2026functional, p. 2].
13	  5. Commercial vibe-coding platforms and IDE agents [@mota2026comparing, p. 2; @he2026speed, p. 4].
14	  6. Behavioural-spec recovery from running apps [@xiong2026propgen, p. 4].
15	
16	  [I] Almost all evaluations run autonomous agents. Practitioner vibe coding is human-steered natural-language prompting with little review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], and it is studied only in small or proxy studies [@mock2026vibe, p. 15; @asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. "Vibe coding" is defined inconsistently across papers, so their results must not be pooled. **Evidence strength: moderate** (consistent descriptive picture; 7 of 23 papers are preprints; fast-moving field).
17	
18	## RQ2: How is functional fidelity of AI-reconstructed or AI-generated applications measured, and how well do current approaches achieve it?
19	- Type: descriptive / comparative
20	- Why it matters: a rebuild is only useful if it behaves like the original; the metrics used decide what "works" means.
21	- Linked objective: O2, O3
22	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
23	- Current answer: Fidelity is measured with four kinds of oracle:
24	  1. Behavioural test replay against the original [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9; @kim2026programdistill, p. 4; @yang2026programbench, p. 5; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
25	  2. LLM or agent judges running natural-language tests [@lu2025webgen, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 4; @chen2025iwr, p. 7].
26	  3. Visual similarity [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4].
27	  4. Navigation graphs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
28	
29	  Fidelity is partial everywhere:
30	  - Full behavioural equivalence is rare: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
31	  - The best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates are about 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
32	  - Interaction logic lags static structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16; @chen2025iwr, p. 16]. chen2025iwr's IFS<VFS gap is partly built into its metrics [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
33	
34	  [I] Scores from different benchmarks use different oracles and are not comparable. **Evidence strength: moderate** for "far from complete; interaction is the bottleneck". **Weak** for any specific figure or cross-benchmark ranking (mostly single runs, 5 of the 8 main fidelity benchmarks are preprints).
35	
36	## RQ3: What is known about the code quality and maintainability of LLM-generated or vibe-coded application code, compared with human-written code?
37	- Type: comparative
38	- Why it matters: rebuilt apps must be maintained; hidden code smells or technical debt would erase the speed gained.
39	- Linked objective: O2
40	- Status: partially answered (evidence conflicting, 2026-11-12)
41	- Current answer: The evidence is mixed:
42	  - Cursor adoption raises project-level SonarQube warnings (+30.26%) and cognitive complexity (+41.64%) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The result is estimator-sensitive (negative and n.s. under Callaway–Sant'Anna) [@he2026speed, p. 16], and the warning rise runs mainly through more code [@he2026speed, p. 8].
43	  - A preregistered RCT found no significant downstream maintainability difference when a second developer evolved AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38].
44	  - GPT-4o code had fewer SonarQube "bugs" than a weak competitive-programming human baseline, with mixed smells [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
45	  - LLM code shows different smell types from human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
46	  - Quality varies by platform [@mota2026comparing, p. 5].
47	  - Rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic than their originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9].
48	  - Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as "fast but flawed" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8].
49	
50	  [I] The measuring instruments disagree (SonarQube, PyExamine, CodeHealth, MI), and no study measures validated maintainability of reconstructed apps against their originals. **Evidence strength: weak to moderate** (conflicting results; see evidence-matrix.md C1–C3).
51	
52	## RQ4: What are the methodological strengths and weaknesses of current evaluations (benchmarks, metrics, sample sizes, baselines, reproducibility) in this area?
53	- Type: methodological
54	- Why it matters: shows how far the reported results can be trusted and how a new study should be designed.
55	- Linked objective: O3
56	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
57	- Current answer: Strengths:
58	  - Implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles with leakage controls [@yang2026programbench, p. 18; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
59	  - Oracle audits [@yang2026programbench, p. 7; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 14].
60	  - Judge–human alignment checks [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @wu2026looks, p. 13].
61	  - One preregistered RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
62	
63	  Recurring weaknesses:
64	  1. Single runs with no variance or significance tests [@lu2025webgen, p. 40; @yang2026programbench, p. 10]. Measured generation variance is large [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
65	  2. Same-family or weakly validated oracles and judges [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @chen2025iwr, p. 17; @si2025benchmarking, p. 17].
66	  3. Uneven contamination handling.
67	  4. Maintainability absent or measured only by proxies [@pan2026functional, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4].
68	  5. Oracles coupled to the original's identifiers, or given structural priors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16; @kim2026programdistill, p. 35; @zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
69	  6. No human-developer baselines in benchmarks.
70	
71	  **Evidence strength: strong** for missing variance and significance testing and for absent maintainability measurement (verified across 12+ papers). **Moderate** for the judge, contamination and oracle-coupling problems.
72	
73	## RQ5: Which gaps remain for jointly evaluating functional fidelity, code quality and maintainability of AI-assisted application reconstruction, and what study design could address them?
74	- Type: methodological
75	- Why it matters: turns the review into a concrete, feasible research contribution.
76	- Linked objective: O4
77	- Status: answered (provisional, after novelty check 2026-11-12)
78	- Current answer: [I] The main gap that survives the novelty check is a joint evaluation of behavioural fidelity and validated, size-normalised maintainability for applications rebuilt from observable artefacts, with the original app as the baseline. We found no study that does this (searches on 2026-11-12). Evidence that the gap exists is strong [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9; @pan2026functional, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4; @tran2026vibe, p. 9]. Five further gaps are partially novel: same-family builder and judge bias, validity of maintainability tools for AI-built apps, feedback effects on fidelity and quality together, the size of the contamination effect, and human-steered vs autonomous reconstruction. Oracles tied to the original's identifiers and native mobile apps with hidden back-ends are mostly or partly addressed by 2026 work. A related security angle (security-control preservation in black-box reconstruction) is partially novel; see reports/novelty-check-security-fidelity.md.
79	
80	  Recommended study: the G1 design in gap-report.md (reference apps of known provenance, ≥3 runs, locator-independent behavioural tests, two static tools plus a maintenance task in the style of borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13]). G2 and G3 are easy add-ons using released Vibe Code Bench outputs [@tran2026vibe, p. 11].
81	
82	  **Evidence strength: moderate** (novelty confidence medium-high for G1; re-check before submission, the field moves monthly).

18	# Echoes of AI: Investigating the downstream effects of AI assistants on software maintainability
19	
20	- Authors: Borg, Markus; Hewett, Dave; Hagatulah, Nadim; Couderc, Noric; Söderberg, Emma; Graham, Donald
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Empirical Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1007/s10664-026-10889-1 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10889-1
23	- Further authors (from metadata.json): Kini, Uttam; Farley, Dave

29	## 1. Research objective
30	Investigate whether co-developing code with AI assistants affects software maintainability, defined as how easily *another* developer can later evolve that code [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- RQ1: Do developers manually evolve code that has been co-developed with AI assistants more efficiently? RQ2: Does code co-developed with AI assistants result in higher quality upon manual evolution? [V] (p. 9).
34	- Four preregistered null hypotheses (non-directional alternatives): no difference in completion time (H0 1), CodeHealth (H0 2), test coverage (H0 3), perceived productivity (H0 4) between developers evolving AI-assisted vs non-assisted code [V] (p. 14).
35	- Note the "RQ1/RQ2" above are the paper's own RQs, not our project RQs.
36	
37	## 3. Methodology
38	- Research design: preregistered (registered report, Borg et al. 2024b) two-phase sequential controlled experiment, following the ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standard for experiments [V] (p. 2, p. 9). Phase 1 (Task 1): participants add a feature to a Java web app with or without AI; assignment to AI-dev / !AI-dev was by stated preference and habitual AI use, not random, so Phase 1 is observational [V] (p. 10, p. 43). Phase 2 (Task 2) is a *randomised controlled trial (RCT)*, i.e. participants are assigned to groups by chance: new participants, all without AI, were randomly assigned to evolve a valid Task 1 solution from either the AI-dev (treatment) or !AI-dev (control) cohort [V] (p. 2, p. 12). Analysis: frequentist tests plus Bayesian causal models built from a DAGitty causal graph, adjusting for Task 1 developer Java skill and habitual AI use (and Task 2 interruptions for completion time) [V] (p. 14, p. 15, p. 16). Qualitative coding of free-text answers and code analysis (CodeScene, PMD, RefactoringMiner) [V] (p. 22, p. 23).
39	- Approach / model / intervention: independent variable = whether the evolved Task 1 code was co-developed with an AI assistant [V] (p. 13). Participants used their preferred tools; reported Task 1 tools: GitHub Copilot 21, ChatGPT 13, Cursor 9, JetBrains AI 5, Claude 4, others ≤2 [V] (p. 27). No fully autonomous agent was given the whole task; usage frequency: every statement 17, often 10, sometimes 12 [V] (p. 25, p. 26). Data collected Oct 2024 – 18 Jan 2025, i.e. before agentic tools became common [V] (p. 3, p. 17).
40	- Baselines or comparison conditions: control = evolving code written without AI in Task 1 [V] (p. 12). Bayesian sensitivity analysis with neutral, AI-sceptical and AI-enthusiastic priors (optimistic completion-time prior from Peng et al.'s 55% speedup) [V] (p. 21).
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): RecipeFinder, a deliberately substandard Java/Spring Boot web app (2 KLoC, 47 files) co-designed with Equal Experts consultants; plus questionnaires and CI measurements [V] (p. 64, p. 65, p. 66).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: 449 valid pre-screening sign-ups (92.2% professional developers, median age group 40–49) [V] (p. 24). 118 assigned to AI-dev, 106 randomly to !AI-dev, 225 reserved for Task 2 [V] (p. 24). Valid solutions: Task 1 = 39 AI-dev + 37 !AI-dev (one !AI-dev reclassified for AI use); Task 2 = 75 (40 treatment, 35 control) [V] (p. 24, p. 25, p. 28, p. 30). Total 151 participants (33.6% of sign-ups) [V] (p. 19). Completion-time analysis uses 72 Task 2 times after removing values >16 h [V] (p. 18, p. 32). Of 75 Task 1 solutions offered, 51 were evolved; 24 were not (similar CH, mean 8.32 vs 8.35) [V] (p. 28). [I] The Task 1 count is inconsistent: 76 (39 + 37) on p. 24 vs 75 on p. 28 (see §9).
45	- Sampling / selection method: volunteers recruited via social media (YouTube, LinkedIn, X) and personal networks; incentive = signed book by the last author and a chance at an "Ask Me Anything" session [V] (p. 10). Stratified random sampling into tasks [V] (p. 10). A priori power analysis (G*Power): 128 Phase 2 participants needed for d = 0.5, α = 0.05, power 0.80; target not reached [V] (p. 19). Sample is 95% male, no participants from China, Japan, South Korea [V] (p. 61).
46	- Data availability (public? link?): Zenodo replication package (task instructions, anonymised data, causal graph; CC BY 4.0) and a GitHub repository with analysis scripts [V] (p. 74). The study code base was deliberately not hosted publicly to avoid leakage into LLM training data; it is shared as PDF documents in the replication package [V] (p. 66). [I] This is in tension with p. 74, which describes "A GitHub repository containing the full code base, scripts for data cleaning and analysis, and notebooks" (p. 74); it is unclear whether "full code base" means the RecipeFinder system or the analysis code.
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: tasks administered via snapcode.review with per-participant GitHub repos; GitHub Actions ran 3 acceptance tests per task, CodeScene (CH) and JaCoCo (coverage), and recorded timestamps [V] (p. 16, p. 17, p. 65). Task 1: add total-time filter to search and fix an injected bug; Task 2: add a cost-per-serving filter on top of a Task 1 solution; quality requirement deliberately vague ("easy to read and maintain") [V] (p. 65). Each Task 1 submission was offered to three Task 2 participants [V] (p. 17). Only solutions passing acceptance tests were kept [V] (p. 17). 73 of 151 (48.3%) did not work in one sitting; 67 self-reported time estimates replaced recorded times; 11 values >16 h removed [V] (p. 18). Bayesian models implemented in Turing (Julia) [V] (p. 67). Phase 1 code analysis: CodeScene v6.19.15, PMD v7.13.0 (default/all Java rules), RefactoringMiner 2.0 [V] (p. 23, p. 66).
50	- Code availability: analysis scripts and notebooks on GitHub, mirrored to Zenodo [V] (p. 74).
51	
52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
54	  - Completion time — time from repo access to final submission; proxy for maintainability because more maintainable code should take less effort to evolve [V] (p. 3, p. 13).
55	  - CodeHealth (CH) — CodeScene file-level score 1–10 penalising 25+ code smells, LoC-weighted average over all files; authors cite prior work showing it correlates with maintenance cost, defects and onboarding and outperforms SonarQube Maintainability Rating and Microsoft Maintainability Index on a benchmark [V] (p. 4, p. 13). Customised for small tasks: Complex Method triggers at cyclomatic complexity 4 (default 9), Nested Complexity at 3 levels (default 4) [V] (p. 13).
56	  - Test coverage (TC) — JaCoCo line coverage; indicator of attention to testing [V] (p. 13).
57	  - Perceived productivity (PP) — 10 five-point Likert items mapped to SPACE dimensions S, C, E [V] (p. 12, p. 14).
58	  - Phase 1 only (exploratory, not preregistered): code smell deltas (removed/improved/unchanged/degraded/introduced), PMD violations, refactoring operations, regex-detected tests/comments/functional style [V] (p. 23, p. 43, p. 45).
59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Shapiro-Wilk normality; Wilcoxon rank-sum + Cliff's δ (time, TC); Welch's t-test + Cohen's d (CH, PP); bootstrap CIs (1,000,000 resamples); no multiple-testing correction [V] (p. 18, p. 19). Bayesian: probability of direction > 95% counted as "significant", 95% credible intervals, posterior predictive simulations [V] (p. 22). Achieved power with n = 75: 80% only for d ≈ 0.66; 0.57 for d = 0.5; 0.17 for d = 0.2 [V] (p. 19). PP internal consistency Cronbach's α = 0.82 [V] (p. 18).
60	
61	## 7. Key findings
62	1. Phase 2 completion time: median 136 min treatment vs 173 min control; Cliff's δ = −0.079 (negligible); Wilcoxon p = 0.56 — [V] (p. 33). Bayesian: P(Δ<0) = 76%, posterior mean −12.59%, CrI [−45.77%, +32.68%]; with a pessimistic prior the probability falls to ~38–39% — [V] (p. 33, p. 34).
63	2. Interruptions dominate Task 2 time: developers who took breaks finished 173.66% later (CrI [+37.69%, +416.88%]) — [V] (p. 34).
64	3. Phase 2 perceived productivity: mean 3.95 vs 4.06; Cohen's d = −0.21; Welch p = 0.37. Bayesian: P(Δ<0) = 84%, mean −1.26 SD, CrI [−2.46, +2.31] for code from habitual AI users — [V] (p. 35, p. 36).
65	4. Phase 2 CodeHealth: mean 8.49 vs 8.44; Cohen's d = 0.28; Welch p = 0.24 (n.s.). Bayesian: code originally AI-co-written by habitual AI users had +0.10 CH after evolution (P(Δ>0) = 98%, CrI [+0.02, +0.19]), stable across priors — [V] (p. 38, p. 39).
66	5. Developer skill mattered more: higher Task 1 Java skill gave +0.16 CH in Task 2 (P > 99%, CrI [+0.07, +0.26]) — [V] (p. 40); authors state Java proficiency had a stronger influence than AI use — [A] (p. 55).
67	6. Phase 2 test coverage: median 0.70 both groups; Cliff's δ = 0.09; Wilcoxon p = 0.49; Bayesian P(Δ>0) = 91%, logit +0.10 (CrI [−0.04, +0.26]) — [V] (p. 42, p. 43).
68	7. Phase 2 smell changes: treatment degraded Complex Method more often (55% vs 31%) and introduced Complex Conditional more often (18% vs 3%); control introduced Primitive Obsession more often (26% vs 8%); the paper calls these "significant" but does not name a test — [V] (p. 38).
69	8. Phase 1 (observational): AI-devs had 30.7% shorter median completion time (Wilcoxon p = 0.0029, Cliff's δ = −0.42); Bayesian estimate for habitual AI users ~60% faster (CrI [−77.11%, −30.64%]) — [V] (p. 33, p. 43). Phase 1 CH: no significant difference (p = 0.52, δ = 0.09) — [V] (p. 44).
70	9. Phase 1 code-level patterns: AI-devs added up to 10,788 lines (mean 642.74 vs 216.41 added lines); resolved the Bumpy Road smell more often (72% vs 46%); introduced more Code Duplication (23% vs 11%), Complex Conditionals (13% vs 5%), Nested Complexity (8% vs 0%); fewer PMD complexity violations but higher variance in Code Style violations (SD 154 vs 45) — [V] (p. 30, p. 45, p. 46, p. 47). Authors: AI use "may reduce complexity but add stylistic clutter" — [A] (p. 47).
71	10. Overall conclusion: no systematic maintainability advantage or disadvantage when others evolve AI-co-developed code; main risks are code bloat and "cognitive debt" — [A] (p. 1, p. 57, p. 58, p. 62).
72	
73	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
74	- [A] Only short-term maintainability is observed; long-term effects need longitudinal case studies (p. 58).
75	- [A] Individual developers only, no team dynamics; small system, so no architectural conclusions; security not studied (p. 58).
76	- [A] Many participants worked in several sittings; time partly self-estimated (p. 18, p. 59).
77	- [A] Possible confirmation bias in AI-devs' perceived productivity (p. 45, p. 59).
78	- [A] Participants' differing definitions of "good enough" quality; randomisation may not balance them at this N (p. 55, p. 59).
79	- [A] Remote setting; protocol adherence cannot be guaranteed; one participant submitted Task 1 twice (p. 17, p. 59, p. 60).
80	- [A] External validity: one small Java/Spring Boot system; Task 2 developers did not use AI; mature commercial assistants only; 95% male, uneven geography (p. 60, p. 61).
81	- [A] RCT underpowered: non-significant results rule out only large effects (p. 61).
82	
83	## 9. Limitations we identified
84	- [I] Phase 1 assignment by preference means the "treatment" is "code from developers who like and habitually use AI, using AI" — not AI use alone. The Phase 2 randomisation protects the comparison of *which code* is evolved, but the treatment effect bundles developer type and tool use. Based on the assignment procedure (p. 10, p. 17).
85	- [I] Internal numeric inconsistencies: the habitual-user Task 1 speedup is 55.9% in the abstract, introduction and conclusion (p. 1, p. 2, p. 62) but ~60% / 59.6% in the results and discussion (p. 33, p. 54); Cronbach's α is 0.82 (p. 18) but ">0.85" (p. 61); the word "habitual" covers two thresholds: AI-dev group assignment required 4 or 5 on Q1-7a plus a preference median >3 (pilot and main phase, "using the same assignment criteria", p. 17), whereas the analysis variable "habitual AI users" means "Strongly agree" only (p. 15). Task 1 valid solutions are given as 39 + 37 = 76 (p. 24), as 38 AI-dev (p. 24) plus 38 !AI-dev (p. 25), and as 75 in total (p. 28); the reclassification of one participant (p. 18, p. 25) explains 38/38 vs 39/37 but not 75 vs 76.
86	- [I] Several Phase 1/Phase 2 smell and PMD differences are called "significant" without a named test or correction (p. 38, p. 47); treat them as descriptive.
87	- [I] The headline "+0.10 CodeHealth" is a Bayesian subgroup result for habitual AI users, at the 95% probability-of-direction threshold, on a scale where groups differ by hundredths; it is the only "significant" maintainability effect and it favours AI.
88	- [I] CodeHealth is a proprietary metric from the first author's employer, customised for this study (p. 13, p. 75); independent replication with an open tool (e.g. SonarQube) was not done for the RCT outcome.
89	- [I] The evolved base system is small (2 KLoC) and Task 2 changes are tiny (median 56.5 vs 80 added lines; some participants called it "simplistic") (p. 52), which limits sensitivity to maintainability differences.
90	- [I] Code volume — the risk the authors themselves highlight — is not an RCT outcome; Task 2 participants were randomised to code bases that varied greatly in size (Task 1 added lines up to 10,788) (p. 30).
91	
92	## 10. Threats to validity
93	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): Phase 2 randomised; Phase 1 not (preference-based) (p. 10, p. 43). Covariate adjustment for Java skill and AI habituality via causal DAG (p. 15, p. 16). Protocol violations handled (p. 17, p. 18). Task code kept out of public repos to prevent LLM training-data leakage (p. 66). Differential dropout: 24 of 75 Task 1 solutions were never evolved (p. 28).
94	- External (generalisability of sample/context): senior professional volunteers, largely Western, male; one Java/Spring Boot app; first/second-generation assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor), late 2024 (p. 3, p. 24, p. 60, p. 61).
95	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): completion time as maintainability proxy is noisy (setup friction, Java ramp-up, interruptions) (p. 53, p. 54); CodeHealth customised thresholds (p. 13); PP self-reported (p. 59).
96	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): underpowered (75 vs 128 planned); no multiple-testing correction; failed sensitivity analysis for completion time under optimistic prior (p. 19, p. 54, p. 61). Independence of observations assumed though some Task 1 solutions were evolved by up to four Task 2 participants (p. 18, p. 28).
97	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): preregistered; Zenodo + GitHub replication package with data, scripts, CodeHealth configuration and task materials (p. 13, p. 74). Conflicts of interest declared: first author employed by CodeScene; three authors consultants at Equal Experts (AI-accelerated delivery); last author runs the YouTube channel used for recruitment (p. 61, p. 75). Funding: open access by Lund University; Vinnova grant 2023-00541 (NextG2Com); WASP (Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation); ELLIIT and Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research grant FFL18-0231 (p. 74).
98	
99	## 11. Future research directions
100	- Stated by authors [A]: study evolution where the second developer also uses AI; evaluate third-generation coding agents (Claude Code, Amp); add security analysis (p. 63); longitudinal case studies and action research on maintainability dynamics (p. 63); examine code bloat from excessive generation and cognitive debt (p. 1, p. 57, p. 62); study when enthusiastic AI use leads to downstream maintainability backlash (p. 62); broaden demographic representation (p. 61).
101	- Suggested by us [I]: run the same two-phase hand-off design with agent-generated (vibe-coded) applications reconstructed from a UI/spec, measuring code volume and system-level structure as RCT outcomes, with an open static-analysis tool alongside CodeHealth.
102	
103	## 12. Relevance to our research
104	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (main), RQ4, RQ5.
105	- How it informs our work [I]: the only randomised evidence in our set on downstream maintainability of AI-assisted code. Its design — a second developer evolves the generated code without AI, with time and quality measured — is directly reusable for evaluating maintainability of reconstructed apps (RQ5). Its null result (no degradation at file level) contrasts with he2026speed's project-level complexity increase; the difference in tool generation (completion/chat vs agentic), scale (2 KLoC task vs real repos) and metric (CodeHealth average vs total cognitive complexity) is a key point for RQ3/RQ4.

28	This is a secondary study. A *multivocal literature review* (MLR) is a literature review that also includes "grey" sources such as blogs, company reports and forums, alongside peer-reviewed papers. In this analysis, "dataset" means the review's source corpus, and "findings" are the review's synthesis of what those sources say, not new measurements.
29	
30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] Examine the forms of technical debt (TD) and their early signs introduced by LLM-assisted development, the risks they bring, and the strategies, tools, metrics and benchmarks available or missing to manage them, from both practitioner (grey) and academic (formal) perspectives (p. 3).
32	- [A] Motivation: prior work on LLM code correctness and quality covers local, task-specific quality but not how issues accumulate into long-term TD (p. 3).
33	
34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
35	- [V] RQ1: What forms of TD are introduced by integrating LLM-generated code into software projects? (p. 7).
36	- [V] RQ2: What strategies or guidelines exist to mitigate TD introduced by LLMs? (p. 7).
37	- [V] RQ3: What tools or techniques exist to detect or measure TD in LLM-generated code? (p. 7).
38	- [V] RQ4: Are there benchmarks or datasets to evaluate the TD of LLM-generated code? (p. 8).
39	- [V] RQ5: Do existing TD metrics sufficiently capture LLM-introduced debt, and if not, what new metrics or dimensions are suggested? (p. 8).
40	- No hypotheses (descriptive review).
41	
42	## 3. Methodology
43	- Research design: [V] MLR following Garousi et al.'s MLR guidelines for SE and Kitchenham et al.'s SEGRESS reporting guidelines (built on PRISMA). Phases: planning, source selection, classification and data extraction, and synthesis (p. 6).
44	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Deductive coding against the 13-type TD taxonomy of Alves et al. (2014), combined with inductive coding for new LLM-specific categories (p. 7, p. 14). Sources are also classified as "direct TD evidence" or "supporting TD evidence" depending on whether TD framing is explicit in the title and main discussion (p. 13–14).
45	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Grey (practitioner) and formal (academic) findings are reported separately and compared for each RQ (p. 14–15). There is no quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis.
46	- Justification for grey literature: [V] Garousi's seven questions (Table 1); the authors answer "Yes" to 5 of 7 and "No" to Q2 ("lack of volume or quality of evidence ... in the formal literature") (p. 7).
47	
48	## 4. Dataset and sample
49	- Source corpus and search:
50	  - [V] Search conducted in January 2026, covering all sources available up to January 2026 (p. 8).
51	  - [V] Final query: any of 13 TD-type terms (technical, code, design, documentation, infrastructure, architecture, test, defect, build, requirement, service, test automation, process debt) AND ("large language models" OR "AI-generated code" OR "LLMs" OR "LLM" OR "ChatGPT" OR "Copilot" OR "AI code" OR "AI assistance") (p. 9).
52	  - [V] The query was developed through exploratory refinement rounds; it was widened from "technical debt" only to all 13 Alves et al. types (p. 8–9).
53	- Grey literature:
54	  - [V] Google via SerpAPI, about 375,000 hits, limited to the first 10 result pages on the basis of relevance saturation (p. 9).
55	  - [V] After de-duplication and removal of academic papers: 132 unique sources (p. 9).
56	  - [V] Quality assessment with 22 binary criteria in 7 categories (authority, methodology, objectivity, date, significance, impact, outlet type), adapted from Garousi; outlet type could score 0.5 (p. 8–9).

138	## 9. Limitations we identified
139	- [I] Frequency of mentions is not strength of evidence. Table 8 counts how many sources mention a debt type (p. 16), mostly from grey sources, and primary-study quality is not weighted. The headline new categories rest entirely on practitioner commentary: governance debt (19 grey, 0 formal) and fast-integration debt (13 grey, 0 formal) (p. 16). They are hypotheses, not established effects.
140	- [I] Fig. 4's y-axis reads "Number of Sources", but grey-source counts for 2025 (84 + 25 = 109) exceed the 73 grey sources (p. 19; values read from the Fig. 4 image, not in the text layer; re-checked 2026-11-12). The figure therefore counts mentions, not sources, which can inflate the visual trend.
141	- [I] No formal quality appraisal of the 31 peer-reviewed sources is described (p. 11–12), although the threats section claims one (p. 29). Weak primary studies (e.g. vision or position papers such as Mitchell et al.'s "Position: Vibe Coding Needs Vibe Reasoning", p. 21, p. 36) are counted like empirical studies.
142	- [I] Inclusion inconsistency: the review restricts formal sources to peer-reviewed work (p. 11), yet Della Porta et al. [157] is listed under EASE in Table 6 (p. 13) while its reference entry gives only an arXiv preprint (p. 36). PromptDebt also appears twice in the references, as a published version [14] and an arXiv version [15] (p. 31).
143	- [I] EC2 excludes papers on correctness or functional quality that do not frame findings as TD (p. 12). Empirical maintainability studies of LLM code that never use the term "debt" (for example SonarQube-based LLM vs human comparisons) may therefore be missing. molison2025llm (ESEM 2025, SonarQube effort-to-fix) does not appear in the reference list; we checked by text search of `fulltext.txt`. The authors partly acknowledge this term-based bias (p. 30).
144	- [I] The grey search covers only the first 10 Google result pages (p. 9), so results depend on Google's ranking at search time. The authors note that the ranking is undocumented (p. 30), and replication is likely to give different results.
145	- [I] Table 1 answers "No" to whether the formal literature lacks volume or quality of evidence (p. 7). This sits uneasily with the review's own conclusion that formal work is "small but growing" (p. 18) and lacks benchmarks and metrics (p. 24).
146	- [I] Grey quality scoring split the 132 sources between two authors with consensus afterwards, and no pre-reconciliation reliability was reported (p. 9). Kappa was computed only for formal-source extraction (p. 13).
147	- [I] The scope is LLM-assisted development in general, not application reconstruction or vibe-coded apps specifically. Vibe coding appears as a cause of fast-integration debt (p. 17, p. 26), and one formal source is a vibe-coding position paper (p. 21).

149	## 10. Threats to validity
150	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [A] Selection bias in screening and search-engine opacity are acknowledged (p. 30). [I] The keyword strategy is anchored on "debt"; with EC2 (p. 12) it selects sources that frame issues as debt, which may over-represent sources that already argue LLMs create debt.
151	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] English only; company blogs dominate (p. 30). [I] The corpus ends in January 2026 (p. 8); the field moves quickly (most sources are from 2025, p. 19).
152	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TD is operationalised as mentions of TD categories. Static-analysis indicators (SonarQube) are treated as "early signs" of TD (p. 22), which is itself an assumption. The review notes that TD tools disagree on what counts as real debt (p. 5).
153	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] Not applicable (no inferential statistics). Counts are descriptive and come from heterogeneous source types.
154	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Search string, databases, date, criteria, QA checklist and per-stage counts are reported (p. 8–12), and annotation sheets are on figshare (p. 4, p. 13). [I] The grey search is hard to reproduce (Google ranking, SerpAPI, first 10 pages). Per-source exclusion reasons at full-text stage are summarised but not itemised in the paper (p. 11).

1	# Research questions — Evaluating AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering for Software Application Reconstruction through Vibe Coding: Functional Fidelity, Code Quality, and Maintainability
2	
3	## RQ1: What AI/LLM approaches exist for reconstructing or generating software applications from observable artefacts (UI screenshots, designs, interaction behaviour, specifications), and how do they relate to vibe-coding workflows?
4	- Type: descriptive
5	- Why it matters: defines what "AI-assisted reverse engineering" currently looks like in practice and research, and which inputs and tools are realistic.
6	- Linked objective: O1
7	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
8	- Current answer: Six approach families exist (see reports/methodology-comparison.md §2):
9	  1. Screenshot or design to code [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @zhou2025declarui, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 6].
10	  2. Interaction video or before/after interaction screenshots to code [@chen2025iwr, p. 5; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
11	  3. Agentic rebuilds from a live running reference or an executable plus docs [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 3; @kim2026programdistill, p. 3; @yang2026programbench, p. 2].
12	  4. Natural-language spec or requirements to a full app [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 3; @lu2025webgen, p. 7; @tran2026vibe, p. 3; @pan2026functional, p. 2].
13	  5. Commercial vibe-coding platforms and IDE agents [@mota2026comparing, p. 2; @he2026speed, p. 4].
14	  6. Behavioural-spec recovery from running apps [@xiong2026propgen, p. 4].
15	
16	  [I] Almost all evaluations run autonomous agents. Practitioner vibe coding is human-steered natural-language prompting with little review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], and it is studied only in small or proxy studies [@mock2026vibe, p. 15; @asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. "Vibe coding" is defined inconsistently across papers, so their results must not be pooled. **Evidence strength: moderate** (consistent descriptive picture; 7 of 23 papers are preprints; fast-moving field).

18	## RQ2: How is functional fidelity of AI-reconstructed or AI-generated applications measured, and how well do current approaches achieve it?
19	- Type: descriptive / comparative
20	- Why it matters: a rebuild is only useful if it behaves like the original; the metrics used decide what "works" means.
21	- Linked objective: O2, O3
22	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
23	- Current answer: Fidelity is measured with four kinds of oracle:
24	  1. Behavioural test replay against the original [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9; @kim2026programdistill, p. 4; @yang2026programbench, p. 5; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
25	  2. LLM or agent judges running natural-language tests [@lu2025webgen, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 4; @chen2025iwr, p. 7].
26	  3. Visual similarity [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4].
27	  4. Navigation graphs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
28	
29	  Fidelity is partial everywhere:
30	  - Full behavioural equivalence is rare: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
31	  - The best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates are about 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
32	  - Interaction logic lags static structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16; @chen2025iwr, p. 16]. chen2025iwr's IFS<VFS gap is partly built into its metrics [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
33	
34	  [I] Scores from different benchmarks use different oracles and are not comparable. **Evidence strength: moderate** for "far from complete; interaction is the bottleneck". **Weak** for any specific figure or cross-benchmark ranking (mostly single runs, 5 of the 8 main fidelity benchmarks are preprints).
35	
36	## RQ3: What is known about the code quality and maintainability of LLM-generated or vibe-coded application code, compared with human-written code?
37	- Type: comparative
38	- Why it matters: rebuilt apps must be maintained; hidden code smells or technical debt would erase the speed gained.
39	- Linked objective: O2
40	- Status: partially answered (evidence conflicting, 2026-11-12)
41	- Current answer: The evidence is mixed:
42	  - Cursor adoption raises project-level SonarQube warnings (+30.26%) and cognitive complexity (+41.64%) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The result is estimator-sensitive (negative and n.s. under Callaway–Sant'Anna) [@he2026speed, p. 16], and the warning rise runs mainly through more code [@he2026speed, p. 8].
43	  - A preregistered RCT found no significant downstream maintainability difference when a second developer evolved AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38].
44	  - GPT-4o code had fewer SonarQube "bugs" than a weak competitive-programming human baseline, with mixed smells [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
45	  - LLM code shows different smell types from human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
46	  - Quality varies by platform [@mota2026comparing, p. 5].
47	  - Rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic than their originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9].
48	  - Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as "fast but flawed" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8].
49	
50	  [I] The measuring instruments disagree (SonarQube, PyExamine, CodeHealth, MI), and no study measures validated maintainability of reconstructed apps against their originals. **Evidence strength: weak to moderate** (conflicting results; see evidence-matrix.md C1–C3).

52	## RQ4: What are the methodological strengths and weaknesses of current evaluations (benchmarks, metrics, sample sizes, baselines, reproducibility) in this area?
53	- Type: methodological
54	- Why it matters: shows how far the reported results can be trusted and how a new study should be designed.
55	- Linked objective: O3
56	- Status: answered (provisional, after methodology comparison 2026-11-12)
57	- Current answer: Strengths:
58	  - Implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles with leakage controls [@yang2026programbench, p. 18; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
59	  - Oracle audits [@yang2026programbench, p. 7; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 14].
60	  - Judge–human alignment checks [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @wu2026looks, p. 13].
61	  - One preregistered RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
62	
63	  Recurring weaknesses:
64	  1. Single runs with no variance or significance tests [@lu2025webgen, p. 40; @yang2026programbench, p. 10]. Measured generation variance is large [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
65	  2. Same-family or weakly validated oracles and judges [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @chen2025iwr, p. 17; @si2025benchmarking, p. 17].
66	  3. Uneven contamination handling.
67	  4. Maintainability absent or measured only by proxies [@pan2026functional, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4].
68	  5. Oracles coupled to the original's identifiers, or given structural priors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16; @kim2026programdistill, p. 35; @zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
69	  6. No human-developer baselines in benchmarks.
70	
71	  **Evidence strength: strong** for missing variance and significance testing and for absent maintainability measurement (verified across 12+ papers). **Moderate** for the judge, contamination and oracle-coupling problems.

73	## RQ5: Which gaps remain for jointly evaluating functional fidelity, code quality and maintainability of AI-assisted application reconstruction, and what study design could address them?
74	- Type: methodological
75	- Why it matters: turns the review into a concrete, feasible research contribution.
76	- Linked objective: O4
77	- Status: answered (provisional, after novelty check 2026-11-12)
78	- Current answer: [I] The main gap that survives the novelty check is a joint evaluation of behavioural fidelity and validated, size-normalised maintainability for applications rebuilt from observable artefacts, with the original app as the baseline. We found no study that does this (searches on 2026-11-12). Evidence that the gap exists is strong [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9; @pan2026functional, p. 3; @wu2026looks, p. 4; @tran2026vibe, p. 9]. Five further gaps are partially novel: same-family builder and judge bias, validity of maintainability tools for AI-built apps, feedback effects on fidelity and quality together, the size of the contamination effect, and human-steered vs autonomous reconstruction. Oracles tied to the original's identifiers and native mobile apps with hidden back-ends are mostly or partly addressed by 2026 work. A related security angle (security-control preservation in black-box reconstruction) is partially novel; see reports/novelty-check-security-fidelity.md.
79	
80	  Recommended study: the G1 design in gap-report.md (reference apps of known provenance, ≥3 runs, locator-independent behavioural tests, two static tools plus a maintenance task in the style of borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13]). G2 and G3 are easy add-ons using released Vibe Code Bench outputs [@tran2026vibe, p. 11].

82	  **Evidence strength: moderate** (novelty confidence medium-high for G1; re-check before submission, the field moves monthly).

18	# Vibe Coding in Practice: Motivations, Challenges, and a Future Outlook – a Grey Literature Review
19	
20	- Authors: Fawzy, Ahmed; Tahir, Amjed; Blincoe, Kelly
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1145/3786583.3786866 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3786583.3786866
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	Note on the source: our PDF is the arXiv v1 (arXiv:2510.00328v1, 30 Sep 2025, stamp on p. 1), a pre-acceptance version with an ACM template placeholder header ("Conference'17", every page); the published ICSE-SEIP 2026 version may differ in wording and pagination. Page refs are to our 12-page PDF.
29	
30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To systematically investigate why users engage in vibe coding, what they experience while doing so, how they perceive the quality of AI-generated code, and which quality assurance (QA) practices they apply, using firsthand accounts in grey literature (p. 1, p. 2).
32	- [A] The authors define vibe coding as "using AI code generation tools to produce software primarily by describing goals in natural language and iteratively prompting, while relying on minimal review of the generated code" (p. 1).
33	
34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
35	- [V] RQ1: What are the motivations behind vibe coding? (p. 2)
36	- [V] RQ2: What is the user experience while vibe coding? (p. 2)
37	- [V] RQ3: What is the perception of the AI-generated code quality with vibe coding? (p. 2)
38	- [V] RQ4: What quality assurance (QA) practices are applied when vibe coding? (p. 2)
39	- No hypotheses; exploratory qualitative design (p. 2).
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Systematic grey literature review (GLR) following Garousi et al.'s guidelines, with a quality-assessment step and Braun & Clarke thematic analysis of extracted "behavioural units" (p. 3, p. 4, p. 5). A *grey literature review* is a systematic review of non-peer-reviewed sources such as blogs and forum posts.
43	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Google search with an iteratively developed search string (six stages, including a pivot to practitioner language and a quasi-gold-standard check), plus backward snowballing (p. 3, p. 4). Each source scored 0-3 on five quality criteria (Authority, Evidence, Objectivity, Currency, Purpose; max 15); sources scoring >= 10 retained (p. 4, p. 5). Quotes extracted at the behavioural-unit level and coded into themes per RQ (p. 5).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (descriptive review; no comparison groups). No comparison against non-vibe-coding or human-written code.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] Grey literature: blog posts, online articles, forums, media articles, technical reports, found via Google (p. 3, p. 5).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 154 sources retrieved; 101 included; 518 behavioural units (140 motivation, 132 experience, 114 code-quality perception, 132 QA practice) (p. 5).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] First 100 results of the final string screened, then screening continued until thematic saturation; snowballing applied to the first 100 results (p. 4). Inclusion: English, 2022-2025, identifiable author, public full text, behavioural evidence of vibe coding (p. 4). 53 excluded: 40 below the quality threshold, 13 by inclusion/exclusion criteria (p. 5). Sources showing "Experienced developers applying critical oversight without skipping QA" were an explicit exclusion criterion (p. 4).
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Replication package on Zenodo, doi 10.5281/zenodo.17188020 (p. 10, p. 11). We did not open it.
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Search with Google; the quasi-gold-standard set comprised posts by Karpathy, Willison, Najim and Shields (p. 4). Quality assessment and unit extraction "mainly conducted by the first author", with "a subset" cross-validated by another co-author (p. 4, p. 5). Exact search date: not reported (reference access dates range from 1 May to 11 August 2025, DD/MM format, p. 11–12). Size of the cross-validated subset: not reported. Inter-rater agreement statistic: not reported. Breakdown of included sources by type: not reported in the text.
54	- Code availability: not applicable (no software); data and analysis in the replication package (p. 10).
55	
56	## 6. Evaluation metrics
57	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Frequency and percentage of behavioural units per theme within each RQ (Tables 2-5) (p. 6, p. 8). These count coded quotes, not sources or people. No code-level measures (correctness, quality, maintainability) are taken.
58	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (descriptive counts only).
59	
60	## 7. Key findings
61	1. [V] Motivation: Speed & Efficiency is the most frequent theme, 87/140 units (62%); Accessibility & Empowerment 20 (14%); Learning & Experimentation 15 (11%) (p. 6).
62	2. [V] Experience: Instant Success & Flow 85/132 (64%); Prompt Struggle & Iteration 17 (13%); Code Breakdown or Abandonment 14 (11%) (p. 8).
63	3. [V] Perceived code quality: Fast but Flawed 78/114 (68%); Fragile or Error-Prone 22 (19%); Sloppy or Low Maintainability 5 (4%); Prototype-Ready Only 5 (4%); High Quality & Clean 3 (3%) (p. 8).
64	4. [V] QA practices: Skipped QA 48/132 (36%); Manual Testing or Edits 38 (29%); Uncritical Trust 24 (18%); Delegated QA to AI 13 (10%); Reprompting Instead of Debugging 6 (5%) (p. 8).
65	5. [A] A "speed-quality trade-off paradox": vibe coders knowingly accept flawed code for rapid progress; only experienced users can fix problems when they arise (p. 9).
66	6. [A] A "QA crisis": most QA practices depart from code verification; vibe-coded apps "may look fine but hide serious flaws" (p. 9).
67	7. [A] A "new class of vulnerable developers" who can build but not debug; practitioners documented vibe-coded apps lacking authentication/authorization or containing hardcoded secrets (p. 9).
68	8. [A] Vibe coding "lowers barriers and accelerates prototyping, but at the cost of reliability and maintainability" (p. 1). This conclusion rests on practitioner perceptions, not on measured code.
69	
70	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
71	- [A] Cannot claim to have captured all relevant grey literature, given its diffuse and evolving nature (p. 10).
72	- [A] Residual quality bias despite the 10/15 threshold (p. 10).
73	- [A] Thematic coding involves subjective judgement; findings are "patterns drawn from the data rather than precise measurements" (p. 10).
74	- [A] Self-selection bias: only practitioners who chose to share stories online; findings not generalisable to all vibe coders (p. 10).
75	- [A] Coding mainly by the first author with subset cross-validation; this "reduced, but did not eliminate" subjective bias (p. 10).
76	
77	## 9. Limitations we identified
78	- [I] Percentages are shares of coded quotes, not of sources or people, yet the Discussion reads them as people: "29% reported that they usually make some manual adjustments" and "19% admitting their code is 'fragile or error-prone'" (p. 9), and "About 14% of vibe coders are motivated" (p. 9), which is 20/140 motivation units (p. 6). One source can contribute several units, so prolific sources may dominate. Based on the unit definition (p. 5) vs the Discussion wording (p. 9).
79	- [I] Excluding "Experienced developers applying critical oversight without skipping QA" (p. 4) removes careful-practice accounts by design, which likely inflates the share of skipped/uncritical QA themes. Inclusion additionally required behavioural evidence such as "AI-generated code used as-is or with light edits, prompting and reprompting, minimal or no testing, review, or improvement" (p. 4), so low-QA behaviour is partly a selection criterion rather than only a finding. The 36% Skipped QA figure is partly a product of the definition and selection.
80	- [I] No code was inspected: all quality and maintainability statements are practitioner perceptions. "Sloppy or Low Maintainability" is only 5 units (4%) (p. 8), so the paper gives little direct evidence on maintainability despite its headline claim (p. 1).
81	- [I] No inter-rater reliability statistic and unknown size of the cross-checked subset (p. 4, p. 5) limit confidence in theme assignment.
82	- [I] Grey-literature authors (bloggers, journalists, vendor staff) may over-report dramatic successes or failures; the source-type mix is not reported in the text.
83	- [I] Inclusion window is 2022-2025 although the term was coined in 2025 (p. 1, p. 4); how pre-2025 "vibe coding" behaviour was identified is not explained.
84	
85	## 10. Threats to validity
86	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Selection shaped by Google ranking, a single search engine, and an exclusion criterion that removes careful QA behaviour (p. 3, p. 4). Mainly single coder (p. 5).
87	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Self-selected online accounts; not representative of all vibe coders (p. 10). [I] English-only, 2025-era tools; tool mix not reported.
88	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Unit frequency measures how often a theme is mentioned, not how prevalent a behaviour is among vibe coders, nor actual code quality.
89	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): not applicable (no inferential statistics); [I] themes with 1-5 units are too thin to interpret.
90	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Search string, criteria, quality rubric and a replication package are reported (p. 4, p. 5, p. 10). [I] Google results are not reproducible over time; exact search dates not reported.
91	
92	## 11. Future research directions
93	- Stated by authors [A]: how practices shift with experience (non-developers, novices, professionals) (p. 10); whether vibe coding produces defect and vulnerability patterns different from conventional AI-assisted and human coding (p. 10); which code review practices (run-and-see, automated tests, AI-assisted review) work under vibe-coding conditions (p. 10); integrating vibe coding into training for non-software developers (p. 10).
94	- Suggested by us [I]: check the perceived-quality themes against actual code (static analysis, tests) for the same projects; count sources or people, not quotes; for our project, test whether a vibe-coded reconstruction of a known app shows the "fast but flawed" pattern on objective fidelity and maintainability measures. Based on the gap between perception data here and the code-level questions in RQ2/RQ3.
95	
96	## 12. Relevance to our research
97	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (characterises the vibe-coding workflow: prompt-iterate, run-and-see, delegate QA), RQ3 (practitioner perceptions of quality/maintainability, not measured), RQ5 (authors' call for empirical defect/vulnerability comparisons).
98	- How it informs our work [I]: gives a practitioner-grounded definition of vibe coding and a description of typical QA behaviour (run-and-see, reprompting) that a reconstruction study should model or control. It does not measure fidelity or code quality, so it can motivate but not support claims for RQ2/RQ3. Venue is peer-reviewed (ICSE-SEIP), but the underlying evidence is grey literature, so weight it as perception evidence only.

21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (published)

28	Note on the source and page numbers: our PDF is the arXiv v1 (arXiv:2602.23905v1, 27 Feb 2026, stamp on p. 1) carrying the MSR '26 ACM header and DOI; it is not the ACM Digital Library copy, so page refs use arXiv pagination. 30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To test whether developer experience still matters in AI-assisted development, i.e. whether "vibe coders with less development experience [can] substitute for expert developers", by comparing agentic pull requests (PRs) of low- and high-experience GitHub users (p. 1).
32	- [V] The paper adopts the definition of vibe coding as "a workflow in which a human developer directs and supervises an AI agent through natural-language prompts and validates the generated code" (p. 1). Operationally, a "vibe coder" is any non-bot user in AIDev who created agentic PRs (p. 2).
33	
34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
35	- [V] RQ1: What is the frequency and magnitude of contributions submitted by high-experience (ExpHigh) and low-experience (ExpLow) vibe coders in OSS? (p. 2)
36	- [V] RQ2: Is the PR merge effort similar between ExpHigh and ExpLow vibe coders? (p. 2)
37	- No formal hypotheses stated.
38	
39	## 3. Methodology
40	- Research design: [V] Retrospective mining study of an existing public dataset of AI-agent PRs, with group comparison and a small manual inspection (p. 2, p. 3). A *mining study* analyses existing repository data rather than running an experiment.
41	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Three steps: select vibe coders and PRs; split them by experience; extract metrics for statistical comparison (p. 2). Experience score = total commits by the user / GitHub account age, retrieved via the GitHub GraphQL API, following Malik et al. (p. 1, p. 2). Users split into quartiles: Q3+Q4 = ExpHigh (859), Q1+Q2 = ExpLow (860) (p. 2). Manual inspection of the top 15 highest-review-volume ExpLow feature PRs to explain friction (p. 3).
42	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] ExpHigh vibe coders are the comparison group for ExpLow (p. 2). No comparison with non-AI (human-only) PRs.
43	
44	## 4. Dataset and sample
45	- Data source(s): [V] AIDev dataset of AI-assisted PRs on GitHub OSS, covering agents such as Copilot, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and Devin; the subset for repositories with >100 stars contains 33,596 PRs and 1,796 users (p. 2).
46	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] After removing bot accounts: 22,953 PRs by 1,719 distinct users (p. 2). Unit of analysis is the PR, grouped by author experience; 11 PR categories (e.g. feature, fix, docs, chore) (p. 2, p. 3).
47	- Sampling / selection method: [V] All non-bot users in the AIDev >100-star subset; bot filter = username contains "bot" or matches known agent identifiers (e.g. Copilot) (p. 2). Selection of the 15 inspected PRs = top review volume in the feature category (p. 3).
48	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] AIDev is public (p. 2); replication package at github.com/AmmarAsdaque/msr-2026-replication-package (p. 2, p. 5). We did not open it.
49	
50	## 5. Experimental setup
51	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Python (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, scipy) (p. 2). Group-wise comparisons "on mean values of each metric across PR categories" (p. 2). Date of AIDev snapshot, agent mix per group, number of repositories, and PRs per user distribution: not reported. Who did the manual inspection and how it was coded: not reported.
52	- Code availability: [V] Replication package on GitHub (p. 5).
53	
54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
55	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Contribution magnitude = commits per PR and files changed per PR (RQ1); PR acceptance rate = merged PRs / submitted PRs; PR resolution time = days from PR creation to merge; PR review volume = total review comments per PR (RQ2) (p. 2). Rationale: "real-world outcomes" of contribution size and merge effort (p. 1, p. 2).
56	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Mann-Whitney U for commits, files, resolution time and review volume; Chi-square for acceptance rate; overall and per category; significance at p < 0.05 (p. 2, p. 3). Benjamini-Hochberg correction "for all tests" (p. 4). Exact p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals: not reported. Group differences are reported as ratios of means (e.g. 2.15x) (p. 2, p. 3).
57	
58	## 7. Key findings
59	1. [V] ExpLow PRs contain 2.15x more commits per PR than ExpHigh (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05); more commits in 10/11 categories, significant in all 10; feature PRs: 1.58 vs 4.20 mean commits (p. 2, p. 3).
60	2. [V] ExpLow PRs change 1.47x more files (p < 0.05); more files in 9/11 categories, significant in 5/11; style PRs: 24.29 vs 70.35 mean files (p. 3).
61	3. [V] ExpLow PRs have a 31% lower acceptance rate (Chi-square p < 0.05); lower in 10/11 categories, significant in all 10; documentation: 93.06% (ExpHigh) vs 75.39% (ExpLow) (p. 3).
62	4. [V] ExpLow PRs take 5.16x longer from creation to merge (p < 0.05); significant in 10/11 categories; chore: 0.61 vs 2.83 days (p. 3).
63	5. [V] ExpLow PRs receive 4.52x more review comments (p < 0.05); significant in 6/11 categories; chore: 0.13 vs 0.86 comments per PR (p. 3). Figure 2c shows average review volume below 1 comment per PR in every category for both groups (p. 4), so the large ratios rest on small absolute numbers.
64	6. [A] Manual inspection of 15 PRs suggests two friction sources: "Infrastructure Mismatch" (AI code that is syntactically correct but ignores build/CI environment constraints) and "Integration Friction" (AI code lacking system context, e.g. privacy schemas), each illustrated by one PR (p. 3, p. 4).
65	7. [A] Low-experience vibe coders "focus on generating more code while shifting verification burden onto reviewers"; managers "may not be able to safely replace experienced developers with low-experience vibe coders without increasing review capacity" (p. 1).
66	
67	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
68	- [A] Findings may not apply under the broader definition of vibe coding as any AI assistance (p. 4).
69	- [A] Experience measured by commit count "conflates activity with skill"; developers with offline experience but few GitHub commits count as low-experienced (p. 4).
70	- [A] Project-specific factors (e.g. review policies) can influence acceptance and review volume; within-category comparison mitigates but residual effects may remain (p. 4).
71	- [A] Multiple comparisons raise Type I error risk; mitigated by Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p. 4).
72	
73	## 9. Limitations we identified
74	- [I] Confounding by repository and agent: ExpLow and ExpHigh users may contribute to different projects (with different review norms) and use different agents (Copilot vs Devin etc.). Neither is controlled or reported (p. 2). Category-level comparison (p. 4) does not control for these.
75	- [I] Unit of analysis / non-independence: the unit of the statistical tests is not stated clearly ("group-wise statistical test comparisons on mean values of each metric across PR categories", p. 2). If PR-level values were tested, the 22,953 PRs from 1,719 users (about 13 PRs per user on average, p. 2) are treated as independent and prolific users or repositories can dominate; no mixed-effects or per-user aggregation is reported. If category means were tested, n = 11 per group and power is very low.
76	- [I] The experience score (commits per account-age, p. 2) is a rate of public activity, not skill; it can also be inflated by AI-agent commits themselves, which may make the split partly circular. Quartile split at the median discards information.
77	- [I] Effect reporting: ratios of means are reported for skewed count/time data while tests are rank-based (Mann-Whitney) (p. 2, p. 3); no effect sizes or CIs. "31% lower acceptance rate" is not stated as relative or absolute, and overall acceptance rates are not given (p. 3).
78	- [I] Resolution time is defined as creation-to-merge (p. 2), i.e. merged PRs only, yet the abstract says ExpLow PRs "remain open 5.16x longer before resolution" (p. 1). Unmerged PRs are not part of this measure.
79	- [I] No code-level quality measure: acceptance, review comments and time are proxies of review burden, not of correctness or maintainability. Calling users "vibe coders" because they opened agentic PRs assumes, but does not verify, the supervise-and-validate workflow of the adopted definition (p. 1, p. 2).
80	- [I] The friction categories rest on 15 PRs and two examples, without a coding protocol (p. 3, p. 4); treat as anecdotal.
81	
82	## 10. Threats to validity
83	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Repository, agent and task-difficulty confounds; possibly non-independent PRs (test unit unclear, see §9); bot filtering by username heuristic may leave automated accounts (p. 2).
84	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] OSS repositories with >100 stars only (p. 2); one dataset; agents of 2025. Does not cover single-developer app building or reconstruction.
85	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] Experience proxy conflates activity with skill (p. 4). [I] Review volume and acceptance are indirect measures of code quality.
86	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied (p. 4). [I] The unit of the tests is unclear (p. 2, see §9): if PR-level, very large N makes small differences significant and clustering by user is ignored; if category means, n = 11 per group gives very low power. No effect sizes either way.
87	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Public dataset and replication package (p. 2, p. 5). [I] AIDev snapshot date and GitHub API retrieval date not reported; account statistics change over time.

89	## 11. Future research directions
