30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To investigate how humans and conversational LLMs (CLLMs) can collaborate "as peers through vibe coding", by comparing four interaction models (solo, collaborative, fully automated, agentic) within a Test-Driven Development (TDD) process (p. 1, p. 2).
32	- [V] Empirical goal (GQM): "Analyse code generation to compare human-CLLM interaction models with respect to code quality and development process efficiency, from the viewpoint of developers, in the context of TDD" (p. 11).
33	- [I] Important for our use: in this paper "vibe coding" means the collaborative model in which the human writes TDD tests and the CLLM writes production code through fixed, scripted prompts that participants could not modify (p. 7, p. 8, p. 15). This is narrower and more structured than the "minimal review" vibe coding of grey-literature definitions (e.g. fawzy2026vibe).
34	
35	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
36	- [V] RQ1: How does the quality of production code vary across interaction models? Sub-questions: RQ1.1 syntactic similarity, RQ1.2 functional correctness, RQ1.3 complexity (p. 11, p. 12).
37	- [V] RQ2: How does the quality of the tests vary? RQ2.1 structural complexity of tests, RQ2.2 coverage (p. 13).
38	- [V] RQ3: How does TDD process efficiency vary? (p. 13)
39	- [V] Statistical null hypotheses per pairwise comparison are one-tailed (H0: A <= B, per Tables 9-13) (p. 25, p. 27); no substantive directional hypotheses stated up front. [I] The reported test directions are not reliable row by row; see §9.
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Two complementary settings: (i) a "controlled pre-experimental study" using a Static-Group Comparison design with a control group (solo-coding, CG) and an experimental group (collaborative, EG) of professionals; (ii) "repeated exploratory executions" of fully-automated and agentic workflows on the same tasks (p. 1, p. 14, p. 15). A *pre-experimental design* is a weak experimental design (Campbell & Stanley) without pre-tests and, in the classical form, without random assignment.
43	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Four interaction models operationalised as workflows (p. 7, p. 8): solo-coding (human only); collaborative (human writes tests, CLLM generates production code; this is what the paper calls vibe coding); fully-automated (scripts drive a single CLLM to write both tests and code); agentic (MetaGPT X platform, Engineer mode) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 17). Prompts built from White et al.'s prompt-pattern catalogue (Game Play, Persona, Template, Context Manager, Question Refinement) (p. 8); prompts tell the CLLM "Built-in functions are not allowed" (Table 7, p. 20). A failing test triggers up to five automatic re-prompts before control returns to the human (p. 19). Each iteration is a new session (p. 22).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Solo-coding (human-only TDD) is the control condition (p. 15). A baseline test suite derived from the specification by category-partition testing is the correctness oracle (p. 11, p. 12).
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] Two development tasks of a Python `TextFormatter` class: centre one word in a line (task 1) and centre two words (task 2), plus a `setLineWidth` setter (Fig. 4, p. 12). Baseline suite: two test methods with 5 and 7 assertions (p. 12, p. 28).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 16 professional developers: 9 solo-coding (P1-P9), 7 collaborative (P10-P16) (p. 16). 5 came from a preliminary experiment (Mock et al. 2025), extended with 11 more (p. 13). Fully-automated: 3 runs (FA1-FA3) (p. 42). Agentic: 12 runs = 2 models (ChatGPT 5, Claude Sonnet 4) x 2 prompt scenarios x 3 runs (p. 42).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] IT professionals from Italy, Denmark and Brazil with TDD and Python experience (p. 15). Recruitment method: not reported beyond this. The authors justify N by the "typical" 15-25 range for studies with professionals (p. 13, p. 15). Participants "randomly assigned" to groups (p. 15). Experience was uneven: many participants had <1 year TDD and/or <1 year Python (Table 5, p. 16). No power analysis reported.
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Toolbox, participant data and questionnaire responses in a GitHub replication package, https://github.com/moritzmock/AI4TDD_journal (p. 43, p. 45). We did not open it.
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Google Colab environment; sessions remote (screen sharing) or in person; 40-minute limit; internet search allowed but not full solutions or independent CLLM use, monitored by observation (p. 15). Collaborative participants could not modify prompts (p. 15). Collaborative and fully-automated workflows used OpenAI GPT-3.5 Turbo via API (p. 14, p. 17). Agentic workflow used MetaGPT X web interface with ChatGPT 5 or Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). Agentic runs pooled across models and prompts after observing "little difference" (p. 17). Time self-reported by humans, measured by runtime (`time` command) for automated workflows (p. 13, p. 17). Iterations not collectable for agentic runs (p. 17). Temperature or other model parameters: not reported. Model version dates/snapshots: not reported.
54	- Code availability: [V] Toolbox and data in the GitHub replication package (p. 43).
55	
56	## 6. Evaluation metrics
57	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] (Table 4, p. 14)
58	  - TPR (Test Pass Rate): share of baseline tests passing on the production code — functional correctness, ISO 25010 sub-attribute (p. 11, p. 12, p. 14).
59	  - MCC (McCabe complexity), SCB/BCB (statement/branch coverage of the production code by the baseline tests) — structural complexity as a maintainability-related attribute (p. 12, p. 14).
60	  - LCS (longest common subsequence) and LED (Levenshtein edit distance) — syntactic similarity between workflows' code (p. 11, p. 14).
61	  - TM (test methods), TAM (assertions per method), SC/BC (coverage of own code by own tests) — test quality (p. 13, p. 14).
62	  - Number of iterations and Time — process efficiency (p. 13, p. 14). CLOC/TLOC reported for size (p. 13).
63	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Kruskal-Wallis H with epsilon-squared effect size as a screen; one-tailed Mann-Whitney U pairwise with Cliff's delta; alpha = 0.05; Holm-Bonferroni correction over six pairwise comparisons per metric (p. 10, p. 11). Confidence intervals: not reported. Means and SDs per group in Table 16 (p. 41, p. 42).
64	
65	## 7. Key findings
66	1. [V] Kruskal-Wallis significant for CLOC, TPR, MCC, BCB, SC, BC and Time; large effects for CLOC (0.34), TPR (0.52), MCC (0.5), Time (0.63) (Table 8, p. 23).
67	2. [V] Functional correctness (TPR): agentic mean 94.58% vs solo 62.0%, collaborative 60.8%, fully-automated 83.3% (Table 16, p. 41, p. 42). Agentic beats every other workflow after Holm-Bonferroni (e.g. agentic > solo: U = 106.5, Cliff's delta 0.97, p = 7.81e-05) (Table 9, p. 25).
68	3. [V] Collaborative (the paper's vibe coding) vs solo-coding: no significant difference in TPR (U = 36.5, delta -0.16, p = 0.314) or MCC (p = 0.479) (Table 9, p. 25; Table 10, p. 27). TPR within humans ranged widely: 8.3% (P7) to 100% (P13); SD 27.3 (solo) and 36.8 (collaborative) (p. 26, p. 41).
69	4. [V] Agentic code is more complex: MCC mean 11.67 vs 6.44 (solo), 6.57 (collaborative), 6.0 (fully-automated) (p. 41, p. 42); significant after correction vs all three (Table 10, p. 27). Baseline branch coverage lower for agentic (mean 65.33%) than solo (83.89%) and collaborative (79.00%) (p. 41, p. 42; Table 10, p. 27).
70	5. [A] The authors interpret the uncovered branches as agent "implementation decisions that are not explicitly defined by the functional specifications", making agentic solutions "architecturally more complex and potentially more difficult to maintain" (p. 35). Not directly measured.
71	6. [V] Agentic code "preserves the main implementation but adds helper methods, logging, and validation"; agentic code shares long common subsequences with other workflows but has larger local edit distance (p. 24).
72	7. [V] Test quality: fully-automated tests always one assertion per method, three methods (p. 28); agentic tests had lower statement and branch coverage than solo tests (SC: U = 88.5, delta -0.64, p = 6.42e-03; BC: p = 7.31e-03), significant after correction (Table 12, p. 30; p. 31). Collaborative test organisation closest to the baseline suite (qualitative) (p. 28).
73	8. [V] Efficiency: agentic fastest (mean 75 s) vs fully-automated 800 s, collaborative 2,057 s, solo 2,266 s (p. 41, p. 42); collaborative participants averaged 12.1 iterations, 5.6 of them needing assertion rework (Table 14, p. 33).
74	9. [A] Choice of interaction model should depend on the objective: agentic for speed and production-code correctness, human-involved workflows for test quality and control (p. 40).
75	
76	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
77	- [A] Human and autonomous workflows were evaluated in different settings (controlled experiment vs repeated executions); comparisons across them need care (p. 36).
78	- [A] Results may be affected by participants' TDD and Python experience (p. 36).
79	- [A] Limited number of professionals reduces statistical power; increasing N was not feasible (p. 13, p. 36).
80	- [A] Instrumentation, baseline test suite, model configuration, TDD process and environment may have influenced the data; not addressed exhaustively (p. 37).
81	- [A] Tasks are simple (p. 37). A single CLLM (ChatGPT via API) for the human-involved workflows (p. 37).
82	- [A] Participants could have used an AI tool on a second screen; cannot be fully ruled out (p. 15).
83	- [A] The agentic part "should be considered exploratory" (p. 17).
84	
85	## 9. Limitations we identified
86	- [I] Model confound: collaborative and fully-automated workflows used GPT-3.5 Turbo (p. 14, p. 17), while agentic runs used ChatGPT 5 and Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). The agentic advantage in TPR and time cannot be separated from the large model-generation gap. The authors call ChatGPT 5 "the most similar" model (p. 17), which we find hard to accept. This undermines the cross-workflow comparison that drives the main conclusions.
87	- [I] Very small groups: 9 vs 7 humans (p. 16), 3 fully-automated runs (p. 42). Repeated runs of the same configuration are not independent participants, yet they enter the same Mann-Whitney tests as people. With n = 3 (fully-automated) the minimum attainable one-tailed p-value is limited, so non-significance there is uninformative.
88	- [I] Design inconsistency: a Static-Group Comparison is, by definition, a design without randomisation, yet participants are said to be "randomly assigned" (p. 14, p. 15); 5 of the 16 came from an earlier preliminary session (p. 13), so session is a possible confound. No pre-test of skill; groups differ in experience (Table 5, p. 16).
89	- [I] Time is self-reported by humans (rounded to minutes, values like 2,400 s) but machine-measured for automated runs (p. 13, p. 41). Differences in Time mix measurement methods.
90	- [I] Two tiny string-formatting tasks with a 12-assertion oracle (p. 12) say little about application-level generation. TPR is assertion-level (e.g. 8.3% = 1/12).
91	- [I] The paper's "vibe coding" condition forbids prompt modification (p. 15) and uses scripted prompts, so it does not represent free-form vibe coding. Conclusions about "vibe coding" should be read as conclusions about this structured TDD workflow.
92	- [I] Some claims go beyond the data: the claim that humans "can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings" (p. 26) rests on single participants (P13: 100%) while the collaborative mean is 60.8% (p. 41). The Related Work states "the agentic workflow statistically produces higher-quality code" (p. 40), which conflicts with the higher complexity and lower coverage reported (p. 27, p. 35).
93	- [I] MCC is the only maintainability proxy; no code smells, readability or static-analysis measures.
94	- [I] Test direction is reported inconsistently. Under H0: A <= B, a negative Cliff's δ should give a large one-tailed p-value, yet several such rows carry small p-values:
95	  - "collaborative > agentic": δ −0.65, p = 8.55e-03 (Table 9, p. 25);
96	  - "fully-automated > agentic": δ −1.00, p = 3.79e-03 (Table 9, p. 25);
97	  - "collaborative > agentic": δ −0.77, p = 3.13e-03 (Table 10, p. 27).
98	
99	  "collaborative > solo-coding" (δ −0.16, p = 0.314, p. 25) is also below 0.5. Other rows are consistent, e.g. "fully-automated > solo-coding" δ −0.15, p = 0.685 (p. 27). This suggests that, for some rows, the reverse alternative was tested and the labels were not updated. The substantive conclusions (agentic has higher TPR and higher MCC) agree with the group means (p. 41, p. 42). Individual p-values should not be quoted without this caveat.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Model generation confounded with workflow (see section 9); session (preliminary vs main) and experience imbalance; self-reported vs measured time. [A] Possible hidden AI use (p. 15).
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Simple tasks, single CLLM for human workflows (p. 37). [I] Python-only, function-level tasks, one agentic platform; results do not transfer to multi-file applications or UI work.
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TPR against a 12-assertion spec-derived suite is a reasonable small-scale functional-correctness oracle; MCC alone is a thin proxy for maintainability; lower baseline coverage of agentic code partly reflects added validation/logging rather than lower quality.
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Holm-Bonferroni correction and effect sizes reported (p. 10, p. 11). [A] Low power acknowledged (p. 36). [I] Non-independent repeated runs pooled as samples; no confidence intervals; one-tailed tests chosen for every direction; reported test directions are inconsistent with the sign of Cliff's δ in several rows (see §9, p. 25, p. 27).
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts (Table 7, p. 20), metrics definitions (p. 14), per-participant data (p. 41, p. 42) and GitHub package (p. 43). [I] Agentic runs via a web interface of a commercial platform are hard to reproduce; model parameters not reported.
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A]: extend to other development practices, CLLMs and agentic platforms (p. 40); investigate whether phase-based and iterative process models remain appropriate when AI can generate complete solutions (p. 40); apply the fully-automated evaluation suite to MBPP and HumanEval (p. 40); study agentic performance under different prompting settings (p. 17); more integrated experimental platforms than Colab (p. 34).
110	- Suggested by us [I]: hold the model constant across workflows; use larger, application-level tasks; measure maintainability with more than MCC (e.g. static-analysis smells, change effort); for our project, reuse the idea of a specification-derived oracle test suite (category-partition) as a functional-fidelity measure for a reconstructed app.
111	
112	## 12. Relevance to our research
113	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (contrasts structured vibe coding with agentic generation), RQ2 (functional correctness measured by a spec-derived baseline test suite), RQ3 (complexity and coverage of AI-generated vs human code), RQ4 (design weaknesses: tiny N, model confound, mixed measurement), RQ5 (no application-level or maintainability-focused evaluation).
114	- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few peer-reviewed controlled experiments that labels its condition "vibe coding" and compares it with human-only and agentic generation. Its evaluation framework (oracle tests for correctness + complexity/coverage for internal quality + time/iterations for effort) is a template our study design could scale up. Its findings are function-level and confounded, so they should not be used as evidence about application reconstruction. Relevance medium for RQ4/RQ5 design lessons, low for direct outcome evidence.

30	## 1. Research objective

35	- [V] RQ1: What are the motivations behind vibe coding? (p. 2)
36	- [V] RQ2: What is the user experience while vibe coding? (p. 2)
37	- [V] RQ3: What is the perception of the AI-generated code quality with vibe coding? (p. 2)
38	- [V] RQ4: What quality assurance (QA) practices are applied when vibe coding? (p. 2)
39	- No hypotheses; exploratory qualitative design (p. 2).
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Systematic grey literature review (GLR) following Garousi et al.'s guidelines, with a quality-assessment step and Braun & Clarke thematic analysis of extracted "behavioural units" (p. 3, p. 4, p. 5). A *grey literature review* is a systematic review of non-peer-reviewed sources such as blogs and forum posts.
43	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Google search with an iteratively developed search string (six stages, including a pivot to practitioner language and a quasi-gold-standard check), plus backward snowballing (p. 3, p. 4). Each source scored 0-3 on five quality criteria (Authority, Evidence, Objectivity, Currency, Purpose; max 15); sources scoring >= 10 retained (p. 4, p. 5). Quotes extracted at the behavioural-unit level and coded into themes per RQ (p. 5).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (descriptive review; no comparison groups). No comparison against non-vibe-coding or human-written code.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] Grey literature: blog posts, online articles, forums, media articles, technical reports, found via Google (p. 3, p. 5).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 154 sources retrieved; 101 included; 518 behavioural units (140 motivation, 132 experience, 114 code-quality perception, 132 QA practice) (p. 5).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] First 100 results of the final string screened, then screening continued until thematic saturation; snowballing applied to the first 100 results (p. 4). Inclusion: English, 2022-2025, identifiable author, public full text, behavioural evidence of vibe coding (p. 4). 53 excluded: 40 below the quality threshold, 13 by inclusion/exclusion criteria (p. 5). Sources showing "Experienced developers applying critical oversight without skipping QA" were an explicit exclusion criterion (p. 4).
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Replication package on Zenodo, doi 10.5281/zenodo.17188020 (p. 10, p. 11). We did not open it.
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Search with Google; the quasi-gold-standard set comprised posts by Karpathy, Willison, Najim and Shields (p. 4). Quality assessment and unit extraction "mainly conducted by the first author", with "a subset" cross-validated by another co-author (p. 4, p. 5). Exact search date: not reported (reference access dates range from 1 May to 11 August 2025, DD/MM format, p. 11–12). Size of the cross-validated subset: not reported. Inter-rater agreement statistic: not reported. Breakdown of included sources by type: not reported in the text.
54	- Code availability: not applicable (no software); data and analysis in the replication package (p. 10).
55	
56	## 6. Evaluation metrics
57	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Frequency and percentage of behavioural units per theme within each RQ (Tables 2-5) (p. 6, p. 8). These count coded quotes, not sources or people. No code-level measures (correctness, quality, maintainability) are taken.
58	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (descriptive counts only).
59	
60	## 7. Key findings
61	1. [V] Motivation: Speed & Efficiency is the most frequent theme, 87/140 units (62%); Accessibility & Empowerment 20 (14%); Learning & Experimentation 15 (11%) (p. 6).
62	2. [V] Experience: Instant Success & Flow 85/132 (64%); Prompt Struggle & Iteration 17 (13%); Code Breakdown or Abandonment 14 (11%) (p. 8).
63	3. [V] Perceived code quality: Fast but Flawed 78/114 (68%); Fragile or Error-Prone 22 (19%); Sloppy or Low Maintainability 5 (4%); Prototype-Ready Only 5 (4%); High Quality & Clean 3 (3%) (p. 8).
64	4. [V] QA practices: Skipped QA 48/132 (36%); Manual Testing or Edits 38 (29%); Uncritical Trust 24 (18%); Delegated QA to AI 13 (10%); Reprompting Instead of Debugging 6 (5%) (p. 8).
65	5. [A] A "speed-quality trade-off paradox": vibe coders knowingly accept flawed code for rapid progress; only experienced users can fix problems when they arise (p. 9).
66	6. [A] A "QA crisis": most QA practices depart from code verification; vibe-coded apps "may look fine but hide serious flaws" (p. 9).
67	7. [A] A "new class of vulnerable developers" who can build but not debug; practitioners documented vibe-coded apps lacking authentication/authorization or containing hardcoded secrets (p. 9).
68	8. [A] Vibe coding "lowers barriers and accelerates prototyping, but at the cost of reliability and maintainability" (p. 1). This conclusion rests on practitioner perceptions, not on measured code.
69	
70	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
71	- [A] Cannot claim to have captured all relevant grey literature, given its diffuse and evolving nature (p. 10).
72	- [A] Residual quality bias despite the 10/15 threshold (p. 10).
73	- [A] Thematic coding involves subjective judgement; findings are "patterns drawn from the data rather than precise measurements" (p. 10).
74	- [A] Self-selection bias: only practitioners who chose to share stories online; findings not generalisable to all vibe coders (p. 10).
75	- [A] Coding mainly by the first author with subset cross-validation; this "reduced, but did not eliminate" subjective bias (p. 10).
76	
77	## 9. Limitations we identified
78	- [I] Percentages are shares of coded quotes, not of sources or people, yet the Discussion reads them as people: "29% reported that they usually make some manual adjustments" and "19% admitting their code is 'fragile or error-prone'" (p. 9), and "About 14% of vibe coders are motivated" (p. 9), which is 20/140 motivation units (p. 6). One source can contribute several units, so prolific sources may dominate. Based on the unit definition (p. 5) vs the Discussion wording (p. 9).
79	- [I] Excluding "Experienced developers applying critical oversight without skipping QA" (p. 4) removes careful-practice accounts by design, which likely inflates the share of skipped/uncritical QA themes. Inclusion additionally required behavioural evidence such as "AI-generated code used as-is or with light edits, prompting and reprompting, minimal or no testing, review, or improvement" (p. 4), so low-QA behaviour is partly a selection criterion rather than only a finding. The 36% Skipped QA figure is partly a product of the definition and selection.
80	- [I] No code was inspected: all quality and maintainability statements are practitioner perceptions. "Sloppy or Low Maintainability" is only 5 units (4%) (p. 8), so the paper gives little direct evidence on maintainability despite its headline claim (p. 1).
81	- [I] No inter-rater reliability statistic and unknown size of the cross-checked subset (p. 4, p. 5) limit confidence in theme assignment.
82	- [I] Grey-literature authors (bloggers, journalists, vendor staff) may over-report dramatic successes or failures; the source-type mix is not reported in the text.
83	- [I] Inclusion window is 2022-2025 although the term was coined in 2025 (p. 1, p. 4); how pre-2025 "vibe coding" behaviour was identified is not explained.
84	
85	## 10. Threats to validity
86	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Selection shaped by Google ranking, a single search engine, and an exclusion criterion that removes careful QA behaviour (p. 3, p. 4). Mainly single coder (p. 5).
87	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Self-selected online accounts; not representative of all vibe coders (p. 10). [I] English-only, 2025-era tools; tool mix not reported.
88	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Unit frequency measures how often a theme is mentioned, not how prevalent a behaviour is among vibe coders, nor actual code quality.
89	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): not applicable (no inferential statistics); [I] themes with 1-5 units are too thin to interpret.
90	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Search string, criteria, quality rubric and a replication package are reported (p. 4, p. 5, p. 10). [I] Google results are not reproducible over time; exact search dates not reported.
91	
92	## 11. Future research directions
93	- Stated by authors [A]: how practices shift with experience (non-developers, novices, professionals) (p. 10); whether vibe coding produces defect and vulnerability patterns different from conventional AI-assisted and human coding (p. 10); which code review practices (run-and-see, automated tests, AI-assisted review) work under vibe-coding conditions (p. 10); integrating vibe coding into training for non-software developers (p. 10).
94	- Suggested by us [I]: check the perceived-quality themes against actual code (static analysis, tests) for the same projects; count sources or people, not quotes; for our project, test whether a vibe-coded reconstruction of a known app shows the "fast but flawed" pattern on objective fidelity and maintainability measures. Based on the gap between perception data here and the code-level questions in RQ2/RQ3.
95	
96	## 12. Relevance to our research
97	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (characterises the vibe-coding workflow: prompt-iterate, run-and-see, delegate QA), RQ3 (practitioner perceptions of quality/maintainability, not measured), RQ5 (authors' call for empirical defect/vulnerability comparisons).
98	- How it informs our work [I]: gives a practitioner-grounded definition of vibe coding and a description of typical QA behaviour (run-and-see, reprompting) that a reconstruction study should model or control. It does not measure fidelity or code quality, so it can motivate but not support claims for RQ2/RQ3. Venue is peer-reviewed (ICSE-SEIP), but the underlying evidence is grey literature, so weight it as perception evidence only.
99

102	|---|---|---|---|---|
103	| RQ1 | Vibe coding defined as natural-language goal prompting plus iterative re-prompting with minimal code review; speed is the dominant motivation (87/140 motivation units, 62%) | p. 1, p. 6 | V | moderate |
104	| RQ1 | Common vibe-coding QA behaviours: skipped QA (36%), uncritical trust (18%), delegating QA to the AI (10%), reprompting instead of debugging (5%) of 132 QA units | p. 8 | V | weak |

108	| RQ5 | Authors call for empirical evidence on whether vibe coding yields defect/vulnerability patterns distinct from AI-assisted and human coding, and on which review practices work | p. 10 | A | moderate |

30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To test whether developer experience still matters in AI-assisted development, i.e. whether "vibe coders with less development experience [can] substitute for expert developers", by comparing agentic pull requests (PRs) of low- and high-experience GitHub users (p. 1).
32	- [V] The paper adopts the definition of vibe coding as "a workflow in which a human developer directs and supervises an AI agent through natural-language prompts and validates the generated code" (p. 1). Operationally, a "vibe coder" is any non-bot user in AIDev who created agentic PRs (p. 2).
33	
34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
35	- [V] RQ1: What is the frequency and magnitude of contributions submitted by high-experience (ExpHigh) and low-experience (ExpLow) vibe coders in OSS? (p. 2)
36	- [V] RQ2: Is the PR merge effort similar between ExpHigh and ExpLow vibe coders? (p. 2)
37	- No formal hypotheses stated.
38	
39	## 3. Methodology
40	- Research design: [V] Retrospective mining study of an existing public dataset of AI-agent PRs, with group comparison and a small manual inspection (p. 2, p. 3). A *mining study* analyses existing repository data rather than running an experiment.
41	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Three steps: select vibe coders and PRs; split them by experience; extract metrics for statistical comparison (p. 2). Experience score = total commits by the user / GitHub account age, retrieved via the GitHub GraphQL API, following Malik et al. (p. 1, p. 2). Users split into quartiles: Q3+Q4 = ExpHigh (859), Q1+Q2 = ExpLow (860) (p. 2). Manual inspection of the top 15 highest-review-volume ExpLow feature PRs to explain friction (p. 3).
42	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] ExpHigh vibe coders are the comparison group for ExpLow (p. 2). No comparison with non-AI (human-only) PRs.
43	
44	## 4. Dataset and sample
45	- Data source(s): [V] AIDev dataset of AI-assisted PRs on GitHub OSS, covering agents such as Copilot, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and Devin; the subset for repositories with >100 stars contains 33,596 PRs and 1,796 users (p. 2).
46	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] After removing bot accounts: 22,953 PRs by 1,719 distinct users (p. 2). Unit of analysis is the PR, grouped by author experience; 11 PR categories (e.g. feature, fix, docs, chore) (p. 2, p. 3).
47	- Sampling / selection method: [V] All non-bot users in the AIDev >100-star subset; bot filter = username contains "bot" or matches known agent identifiers (e.g. Copilot) (p. 2). Selection of the 15 inspected PRs = top review volume in the feature category (p. 3).
48	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] AIDev is public (p. 2); replication package at github.com/AmmarAsdaque/msr-2026-replication-package (p. 2, p. 5). We did not open it.
49	
50	## 5. Experimental setup
51	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Python (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, scipy) (p. 2). Group-wise comparisons "on mean values of each metric across PR categories" (p. 2). Date of AIDev snapshot, agent mix per group, number of repositories, and PRs per user distribution: not reported. Who did the manual inspection and how it was coded: not reported.
52	- Code availability: [V] Replication package on GitHub (p. 5).
53	
54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
55	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Contribution magnitude = commits per PR and files changed per PR (RQ1); PR acceptance rate = merged PRs / submitted PRs; PR resolution time = days from PR creation to merge; PR review volume = total review comments per PR (RQ2) (p. 2). Rationale: "real-world outcomes" of contribution size and merge effort (p. 1, p. 2).
56	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Mann-Whitney U for commits, files, resolution time and review volume; Chi-square for acceptance rate; overall and per category; significance at p < 0.05 (p. 2, p. 3). Benjamini-Hochberg correction "for all tests" (p. 4). Exact p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals: not reported. Group differences are reported as ratios of means (e.g. 2.15x) (p. 2, p. 3).
57	
58	## 7. Key findings
59	1. [V] ExpLow PRs contain 2.15x more commits per PR than ExpHigh (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05); more commits in 10/11 categories, significant in all 10; feature PRs: 1.58 vs 4.20 mean commits (p. 2, p. 3).
60	2. [V] ExpLow PRs change 1.47x more files (p < 0.05); more files in 9/11 categories, significant in 5/11; style PRs: 24.29 vs 70.35 mean files (p. 3).
61	3. [V] ExpLow PRs have a 31% lower acceptance rate (Chi-square p < 0.05); lower in 10/11 categories, significant in all 10; documentation: 93.06% (ExpHigh) vs 75.39% (ExpLow) (p. 3).
62	4. [V] ExpLow PRs take 5.16x longer from creation to merge (p < 0.05); significant in 10/11 categories; chore: 0.61 vs 2.83 days (p. 3).
63	5. [V] ExpLow PRs receive 4.52x more review comments (p < 0.05); significant in 6/11 categories; chore: 0.13 vs 0.86 comments per PR (p. 3). Figure 2c shows average review volume below 1 comment per PR in every category for both groups (p. 4), so the large ratios rest on small absolute numbers.
64	6. [A] Manual inspection of 15 PRs suggests two friction sources: "Infrastructure Mismatch" (AI code that is syntactically correct but ignores build/CI environment constraints) and "Integration Friction" (AI code lacking system context, e.g. privacy schemas), each illustrated by one PR (p. 3, p. 4).
65	7. [A] Low-experience vibe coders "focus on generating more code while shifting verification burden onto reviewers"; managers "may not be able to safely replace experienced developers with low-experience vibe coders without increasing review capacity" (p. 1).
66	
67	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
68	- [A] Findings may not apply under the broader definition of vibe coding as any AI assistance (p. 4).
69	- [A] Experience measured by commit count "conflates activity with skill"; developers with offline experience but few GitHub commits count as low-experienced (p. 4).
70	- [A] Project-specific factors (e.g. review policies) can influence acceptance and review volume; within-category comparison mitigates but residual effects may remain (p. 4).
71	- [A] Multiple comparisons raise Type I error risk; mitigated by Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p. 4).
72	
73	## 9. Limitations we identified
74	- [I] Confounding by repository and agent: ExpLow and ExpHigh users may contribute to different projects (with different review norms) and use different agents (Copilot vs Devin etc.). Neither is controlled or reported (p. 2). Category-level comparison (p. 4) does not control for these.
75	- [I] Unit of analysis / non-independence: the unit of the statistical tests is not stated clearly ("group-wise statistical test comparisons on mean values of each metric across PR categories", p. 2). If PR-level values were tested, the 22,953 PRs from 1,719 users (about 13 PRs per user on average, p. 2) are treated as independent and prolific users or repositories can dominate; no mixed-effects or per-user aggregation is reported. If category means were tested, n = 11 per group and power is very low.
76	- [I] The experience score (commits per account-age, p. 2) is a rate of public activity, not skill; it can also be inflated by AI-agent commits themselves, which may make the split partly circular. Quartile split at the median discards information.
77	- [I] Effect reporting: ratios of means are reported for skewed count/time data while tests are rank-based (Mann-Whitney) (p. 2, p. 3); no effect sizes or CIs. "31% lower acceptance rate" is not stated as relative or absolute, and overall acceptance rates are not given (p. 3).
78	- [I] Resolution time is defined as creation-to-merge (p. 2), i.e. merged PRs only, yet the abstract says ExpLow PRs "remain open 5.16x longer before resolution" (p. 1). Unmerged PRs are not part of this measure.
79	- [I] No code-level quality measure: acceptance, review comments and time are proxies of review burden, not of correctness or maintainability. Calling users "vibe coders" because they opened agentic PRs assumes, but does not verify, the supervise-and-validate workflow of the adopted definition (p. 1, p. 2).
80	- [I] The friction categories rest on 15 PRs and two examples, without a coding protocol (p. 3, p. 4); treat as anecdotal.
81	
82	## 10. Threats to validity
83	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Repository, agent and task-difficulty confounds; possibly non-independent PRs (test unit unclear, see §9); bot filtering by username heuristic may leave automated accounts (p. 2).
84	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] OSS repositories with >100 stars only (p. 2); one dataset; agents of 2025. Does not cover single-developer app building or reconstruction.
85	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] Experience proxy conflates activity with skill (p. 4). [I] Review volume and acceptance are indirect measures of code quality.
86	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied (p. 4). [I] The unit of the tests is unclear (p. 2, see §9): if PR-level, very large N makes small differences significant and clustering by user is ignored; if category means, n = 11 per group gives very low power. No effect sizes either way.
87	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Public dataset and replication package (p. 2, p. 5). [I] AIDev snapshot date and GitHub API retrieval date not reported; account statistics change over time.
88	
89	## 11. Future research directions
90	- Stated by authors [A]: extend the ExpHigh vs ExpLow lens to industrial settings and longitudinal studies to see how AI's role evolves with experience, informing adaptive AI tools, reviewer automation and task assignment (p. 4); training that emphasises verification skills (p. 4).
91	- Suggested by us [I]: control for repository and agent with mixed-effects models; add code-level quality measures (static analysis, defects after merge) to separate review friction from code quality; for our project, record and control the operator's experience level when evaluating vibe-coded reconstructions.
92	
93	## 12. Relevance to our research
94	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (indirect: review burden and acceptance of AI-agent code as quality proxies), RQ4 (proxy metrics, clustering, experience operationalisation), RQ5 (operator experience as a variable a reconstruction study should control).
95	- How it informs our work [I]: shows that outcomes of AI-generated contributions differ with the human operator's experience, so a study of vibe-coded app reconstruction should fix or measure operator expertise. It does not evaluate application reconstruction, functional fidelity or code quality directly, hence relevance low. Peer-reviewed 5-page paper at MSR 2026 (track not stated in the PDF; a 5-page format suggests a short or challenge-track paper, which would be a lower tier than a technical-track paper, but this is unchecked) with large N but weak construct validity.

18	# Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development
19	
20	- Authors: Mock, Moritz; Russo, Barbara
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Empirical Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1007/s10664-026-10950-z · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10950-z
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	Note on the source: the PDF analysed is the published Springer open-access version of record (link.springer.com, DOI above; not the arXiv preprint 2607.22406) (Empirical Software Engineering (2027) 32:40, accepted 4 August 2026; 48 pages). Metadata gives year 2026 (online publication); the printed volume year is 2027 (p. 1).
29	
30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To investigate how humans and conversational LLMs (CLLMs) can collaborate "as peers through vibe coding", by comparing four interaction models (solo, collaborative, fully automated, agentic) within a Test-Driven Development (TDD) process (p. 1, p. 2).
32	- [V] Empirical goal (GQM): "Analyse code generation to compare human-CLLM interaction models with respect to code quality and development process efficiency, from the viewpoint of developers, in the context of TDD" (p. 11).
33	- [I] Important for our use: in this paper "vibe coding" means the collaborative model in which the human writes TDD tests and the CLLM writes production code through fixed, scripted prompts that participants could not modify (p. 7, p. 8, p. 15). This is narrower and more structured than the "minimal review" vibe coding of grey-literature definitions (e.g. fawzy2026vibe).
34	
35	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
36	- [V] RQ1: How does the quality of production code vary across interaction models? Sub-questions: RQ1.1 syntactic similarity, RQ1.2 functional correctness, RQ1.3 complexity (p. 11, p. 12).
37	- [V] RQ2: How does the quality of the tests vary? RQ2.1 structural complexity of tests, RQ2.2 coverage (p. 13).
38	- [V] RQ3: How does TDD process efficiency vary? (p. 13)
39	- [V] Statistical null hypotheses per pairwise comparison are one-tailed (H0: A <= B, per Tables 9-13) (p. 25, p. 27); no substantive directional hypotheses stated up front. [I] The reported test directions are not reliable row by row; see §9.
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Two complementary settings: (i) a "controlled pre-experimental study" using a Static-Group Comparison design with a control group (solo-coding, CG) and an experimental group (collaborative, EG) of professionals; (ii) "repeated exploratory executions" of fully-automated and agentic workflows on the same tasks (p. 1, p. 14, p. 15). A *pre-experimental design* is a weak experimental design (Campbell & Stanley) without pre-tests and, in the classical form, without random assignment.
43	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Four interaction models operationalised as workflows (p. 7, p. 8): solo-coding (human only); collaborative (human writes tests, CLLM generates production code; this is what the paper calls vibe coding); fully-automated (scripts drive a single CLLM to write both tests and code); agentic (MetaGPT X platform, Engineer mode) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 17). Prompts built from White et al.'s prompt-pattern catalogue (Game Play, Persona, Template, Context Manager, Question Refinement) (p. 8); prompts tell the CLLM "Built-in functions are not allowed" (Table 7, p. 20). A failing test triggers up to five automatic re-prompts before control returns to the human (p. 19). Each iteration is a new session (p. 22).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Solo-coding (human-only TDD) is the control condition (p. 15). A baseline test suite derived from the specification by category-partition testing is the correctness oracle (p. 11, p. 12).
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] Two development tasks of a Python `TextFormatter` class: centre one word in a line (task 1) and centre two words (task 2), plus a `setLineWidth` setter (Fig. 4, p. 12). Baseline suite: two test methods with 5 and 7 assertions (p. 12, p. 28).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 16 professional developers: 9 solo-coding (P1-P9), 7 collaborative (P10-P16) (p. 16). 5 came from a preliminary experiment (Mock et al. 2025), extended with 11 more (p. 13). Fully-automated: 3 runs (FA1-FA3) (p. 42). Agentic: 12 runs = 2 models (ChatGPT 5, Claude Sonnet 4) x 2 prompt scenarios x 3 runs (p. 42).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] IT professionals from Italy, Denmark and Brazil with TDD and Python experience (p. 15). Recruitment method: not reported beyond this. The authors justify N by the "typical" 15-25 range for studies with professionals (p. 13, p. 15). Participants "randomly assigned" to groups (p. 15). Experience was uneven: many participants had <1 year TDD and/or <1 year Python (Table 5, p. 16). No power analysis reported.
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Toolbox, participant data and questionnaire responses in a GitHub replication package, https://github.com/moritzmock/AI4TDD_journal (p. 43, p. 45). We did not open it.
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Google Colab environment; sessions remote (screen sharing) or in person; 40-minute limit; internet search allowed but not full solutions or independent CLLM use, monitored by observation (p. 15). Collaborative participants could not modify prompts (p. 15). Collaborative and fully-automated workflows used OpenAI GPT-3.5 Turbo via API (p. 14, p. 17). Agentic workflow used MetaGPT X web interface with ChatGPT 5 or Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). Agentic runs pooled across models and prompts after observing "little difference" (p. 17). Time self-reported by humans, measured by runtime (`time` command) for automated workflows (p. 13, p. 17). Iterations not collectable for agentic runs (p. 17). Temperature or other model parameters: not reported. Model version dates/snapshots: not reported.
54	- Code availability: [V] Toolbox and data in the GitHub replication package (p. 43).
55	
56	## 6. Evaluation metrics
57	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] (Table 4, p. 14)
58	  - TPR (Test Pass Rate): share of baseline tests passing on the production code — functional correctness, ISO 25010 sub-attribute (p. 11, p. 12, p. 14).
59	  - MCC (McCabe complexity), SCB/BCB (statement/branch coverage of the production code by the baseline tests) — structural complexity as a maintainability-related attribute (p. 12, p. 14).
60	  - LCS (longest common subsequence) and LED (Levenshtein edit distance) — syntactic similarity between workflows' code (p. 11, p. 14).
61	  - TM (test methods), TAM (assertions per method), SC/BC (coverage of own code by own tests) — test quality (p. 13, p. 14).
62	  - Number of iterations and Time — process efficiency (p. 13, p. 14). CLOC/TLOC reported for size (p. 13).
63	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Kruskal-Wallis H with epsilon-squared effect size as a screen; one-tailed Mann-Whitney U pairwise with Cliff's delta; alpha = 0.05; Holm-Bonferroni correction over six pairwise comparisons per metric (p. 10, p. 11). Confidence intervals: not reported. Means and SDs per group in Table 16 (p. 41, p. 42).
64	
65	## 7. Key findings
66	1. [V] Kruskal-Wallis significant for CLOC, TPR, MCC, BCB, SC, BC and Time; large effects for CLOC (0.34), TPR (0.52), MCC (0.5), Time (0.63) (Table 8, p. 23).
67	2. [V] Functional correctness (TPR): agentic mean 94.58% vs solo 62.0%, collaborative 60.8%, fully-automated 83.3% (Table 16, p. 41, p. 42). Agentic beats every other workflow after Holm-Bonferroni (e.g. agentic > solo: U = 106.5, Cliff's delta 0.97, p = 7.81e-05) (Table 9, p. 25).
68	3. [V] Collaborative (the paper's vibe coding) vs solo-coding: no significant difference in TPR (U = 36.5, delta -0.16, p = 0.314) or MCC (p = 0.479) (Table 9, p. 25; Table 10, p. 27). TPR within humans ranged widely: 8.3% (P7) to 100% (P13); SD 27.3 (solo) and 36.8 (collaborative) (p. 26, p. 41).
69	4. [V] Agentic code is more complex: MCC mean 11.67 vs 6.44 (solo), 6.57 (collaborative), 6.0 (fully-automated) (p. 41, p. 42); significant after correction vs all three (Table 10, p. 27). Baseline branch coverage lower for agentic (mean 65.33%) than solo (83.89%) and collaborative (79.00%) (p. 41, p. 42; Table 10, p. 27).
70	5. [A] The authors interpret the uncovered branches as agent "implementation decisions that are not explicitly defined by the functional specifications", making agentic solutions "architecturally more complex and potentially more difficult to maintain" (p. 35). Not directly measured.
71	6. [V] Agentic code "preserves the main implementation but adds helper methods, logging, and validation"; agentic code shares long common subsequences with other workflows but has larger local edit distance (p. 24).
72	7. [V] Test quality: fully-automated tests always one assertion per method, three methods (p. 28); agentic tests had lower statement and branch coverage than solo tests (SC: U = 88.5, delta -0.64, p = 6.42e-03; BC: p = 7.31e-03), significant after correction (Table 12, p. 30; p. 31). Collaborative test organisation closest to the baseline suite (qualitative) (p. 28).
73	8. [V] Efficiency: agentic fastest (mean 75 s) vs fully-automated 800 s, collaborative 2,057 s, solo 2,266 s (p. 41, p. 42); collaborative participants averaged 12.1 iterations, 5.6 of them needing assertion rework (Table 14, p. 33).
74	9. [A] Choice of interaction model should depend on the objective: agentic for speed and production-code correctness, human-involved workflows for test quality and control (p. 40).
75	
76	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
77	- [A] Human and autonomous workflows were evaluated in different settings (controlled experiment vs repeated executions); comparisons across them need care (p. 36).
78	- [A] Results may be affected by participants' TDD and Python experience (p. 36).
79	- [A] Limited number of professionals reduces statistical power; increasing N was not feasible (p. 13, p. 36).
80	- [A] Instrumentation, baseline test suite, model configuration, TDD process and environment may have influenced the data; not addressed exhaustively (p. 37).
81	- [A] Tasks are simple (p. 37). A single CLLM (ChatGPT via API) for the human-involved workflows (p. 37).
82	- [A] Participants could have used an AI tool on a second screen; cannot be fully ruled out (p. 15).
83	- [A] The agentic part "should be considered exploratory" (p. 17).
84	
85	## 9. Limitations we identified
86	- [I] Model confound: collaborative and fully-automated workflows used GPT-3.5 Turbo (p. 14, p. 17), while agentic runs used ChatGPT 5 and Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). The agentic advantage in TPR and time cannot be separated from the large model-generation gap. The authors call ChatGPT 5 "the most similar" model (p. 17), which we find hard to accept. This undermines the cross-workflow comparison that drives the main conclusions.
87	- [I] Very small groups: 9 vs 7 humans (p. 16), 3 fully-automated runs (p. 42). Repeated runs of the same configuration are not independent participants, yet they enter the same Mann-Whitney tests as people. With n = 3 (fully-automated) the minimum attainable one-tailed p-value is limited, so non-significance there is uninformative.
88	- [I] Design inconsistency: a Static-Group Comparison is, by definition, a design without randomisation, yet participants are said to be "randomly assigned" (p. 14, p. 15); 5 of the 16 came from an earlier preliminary session (p. 13), so session is a possible confound. No pre-test of skill; groups differ in experience (Table 5, p. 16).
89	- [I] Time is self-reported by humans (rounded to minutes, values like 2,400 s) but machine-measured for automated runs (p. 13, p. 41). Differences in Time mix measurement methods.
90	- [I] Two tiny string-formatting tasks with a 12-assertion oracle (p. 12) say little about application-level generation. TPR is assertion-level (e.g. 8.3% = 1/12).
91	- [I] The paper's "vibe coding" condition forbids prompt modification (p. 15) and uses scripted prompts, so it does not represent free-form vibe coding. Conclusions about "vibe coding" should be read as conclusions about this structured TDD workflow.
92	- [I] Some claims go beyond the data: the claim that humans "can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings" (p. 26) rests on single participants (P13: 100%) while the collaborative mean is 60.8% (p. 41). The Related Work states "the agentic workflow statistically produces higher-quality code" (p. 40), which conflicts with the higher complexity and lower coverage reported (p. 27, p. 35).
93	- [I] MCC is the only maintainability proxy; no code smells, readability or static-analysis measures.
94	- [I] Test direction is reported inconsistently. Under H0: A <= B, a negative Cliff's δ should give a large one-tailed p-value, yet several such rows carry small p-values:
95	  - "collaborative > agentic": δ −0.65, p = 8.55e-03 (Table 9, p. 25);
96	  - "fully-automated > agentic": δ −1.00, p = 3.79e-03 (Table 9, p. 25);
97	  - "collaborative > agentic": δ −0.77, p = 3.13e-03 (Table 10, p. 27).
98	
99	  "collaborative > solo-coding" (δ −0.16, p = 0.314, p. 25) is also below 0.5. Other rows are consistent, e.g. "fully-automated > solo-coding" δ −0.15, p = 0.685 (p. 27). This suggests that, for some rows, the reverse alternative was tested and the labels were not updated. The substantive conclusions (agentic has higher TPR and higher MCC) agree with the group means (p. 41, p. 42). Individual p-values should not be quoted without this caveat.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Model generation confounded with workflow (see section 9); session (preliminary vs main) and experience imbalance; self-reported vs measured time. [A] Possible hidden AI use (p. 15).
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Simple tasks, single CLLM for human workflows (p. 37). [I] Python-only, function-level tasks, one agentic platform; results do not transfer to multi-file applications or UI work.
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TPR against a 12-assertion spec-derived suite is a reasonable small-scale functional-correctness oracle; MCC alone is a thin proxy for maintainability; lower baseline coverage of agentic code partly reflects added validation/logging rather than lower quality.
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Holm-Bonferroni correction and effect sizes reported (p. 10, p. 11). [A] Low power acknowledged (p. 36). [I] Non-independent repeated runs pooled as samples; no confidence intervals; one-tailed tests chosen for every direction; reported test directions are inconsistent with the sign of Cliff's δ in several rows (see §9, p. 25, p. 27).
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts (Table 7, p. 20), metrics definitions (p. 14), per-participant data (p. 41, p. 42) and GitHub package (p. 43). [I] Agentic runs via a web interface of a commercial platform are hard to reproduce; model parameters not reported.
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A]: extend to other development practices, CLLMs and agentic platforms (p. 40); investigate whether phase-based and iterative process models remain appropriate when AI can generate complete solutions (p. 40); apply the fully-automated evaluation suite to MBPP and HumanEval (p. 40); study agentic performance under different prompting settings (p. 17); more integrated experimental platforms than Colab (p. 34).
110	- Suggested by us [I]: hold the model constant across workflows; use larger, application-level tasks; measure maintainability with more than MCC (e.g. static-analysis smells, change effort); for our project, reuse the idea of a specification-derived oracle test suite (category-partition) as a functional-fidelity measure for a reconstructed app.
111	
112	## 12. Relevance to our research
113	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (contrasts structured vibe coding with agentic generation), RQ2 (functional correctness measured by a spec-derived baseline test suite), RQ3 (complexity and coverage of AI-generated vs human code), RQ4 (design weaknesses: tiny N, model confound, mixed measurement), RQ5 (no application-level or maintainability-focused evaluation).
114	- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few peer-reviewed controlled experiments that labels its condition "vibe coding" and compares it with human-only and agentic generation. Its evaluation framework (oracle tests for correctness + complexity/coverage for internal quality + time/iterations for effort) is a template our study design could scale up. Its findings are function-level and confounded, so they should not be used as evidence about application reconstruction. Relevance medium for RQ4/RQ5 design lessons, low for direct outcome evidence.
115	
116	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
117	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
118	|---|---|---|---|---|
119	| RQ1 | "Vibe coding" operationalised as human-written TDD tests plus CLLM-generated code via fixed scripted prompts; agentic coding via MetaGPT X as the autonomous contrast | p. 7, p. 8, p. 15, p. 17 | V | moderate |
120	| RQ2 | Agentic runs passed more spec-derived baseline tests (mean TPR 94.58%) than solo (62.0%), collaborative (60.8%) and fully-automated (83.3%) workflows; significant after Holm-Bonferroni, but agentic used newer models (GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4 vs GPT-3.5 Turbo) | p. 25, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
121	| RQ2 | Collaborative vibe coding did not differ significantly from solo human coding in functional correctness (TPR p = 0.314); human results varied from 8.3% to 100% | p. 25, p. 41 | V | weak |
122	| RQ3 | Agentic code had higher McCabe complexity (mean 11.67 vs about 6-6.6 for other workflows) and lower baseline branch coverage (65.3% vs 79-84% for human workflows), adding helpers, logging and validation | p. 24, p. 27, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
123	| RQ3 | Authors argue agentic solutions are architecturally more complex and "potentially more difficult to maintain"; maintainability not directly measured | p. 35 | A | weak |
124	| RQ4 | Evaluation used spec-derived category-partition oracle tests, MCC, coverage, LCS/LED similarity, iterations and time, with Kruskal-Wallis, one-tailed Mann-Whitney, Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni | p. 10, p. 11, p. 14 | V | moderate |
125	| RQ4 | Sample: 9 solo vs 7 collaborative professionals, 3 fully-automated and 12 agentic runs; 2 small Python tasks; time self-reported for humans but measured for automated runs | p. 12, p. 13, p. 16, p. 42 | V | moderate |
126	
127	## 14. Key quotes
128	> "The solutions produced by the agentic workflow show the highest functional correctness, although human developers can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings." (p. 26)
129	
130	> "autonomous agentic platforms can effectively solve development tasks while generating solutions that are architecturally more complex and potentially more difficult to maintain" (p. 35)
131	
132	> "Nonetheless, the limited number of professional participants reduces the statistical power of our analyses." (p. 36)
133	
134	## Analyst notes
135	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1-43), including appendix Table 16 (pp. 41-42) and declarations (p. 43). Fig. 4 (task specification, p. 12) and Table 7 (prompts, p. 20) read from the PDF images because the text layer omits them. Figures 1-3, 5-11 (diagrams/boxplots) not inspected beyond captions and text. Reference list (pp. 43-48) only checked for the replication package. Replication package not opened.
136	- Uncertainties: whether "randomly assigned" (p. 15) applied to all 16 or only to the 11 new participants is not stated. Agentic TPR values in Table 16 (83.0, 92.0) do not exactly equal multiples of 1/12 (83.3, 91.7), suggesting rounding or a different baseline count for agentic runs; not explained. Funding: EU NextGenerationEU / PRIN2022; authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 43).
137

145:| RQ4 | SonarQube and general linters are the main measurement tools, but they are not designed for LLM-specific debt; candidate LLM-specific metrics (PSC, AUP/DUR, data-smell strength/density) are early and not standardised | [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22; @ehsani2026faster, pp. 24–25; @ehsani2026faster, p. 28] | [A] | Multivocal review; 31 formal + 73 grey sources | moderate |  |

218	| RQ5 | Authors call for semantic-cohesion metrics, longitudinal evolution benchmarks and architecture-aware/refactoring agents | [@zhu2026understanding, p. 10] | [A] | Exploratory static analysis; 90 problems x 5 LLMs; ~20 MetaGPT apps | weak |  |
219	
220	## Contradictions
221	<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->
222	
223	Each entry records both sides with page refs, then compares data, population, method, metric and time. Explanations are labelled [I]. We do not pick a side.
224	
225	### C1. Does AI assistance harm maintainability? he2026speed vs borg2026echoes
226	- **Side A** [V]: Cursor adoption in 806 OSS repositories raised total SonarQube static-analysis warnings by +30.26% and total cognitive complexity by +41.64% relative to matched controls (Borusyak DiD) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The complexity effect stays significant after controlling for codebase size in the GMM (0.086, p<0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
227	- **Side B** [V]: When a second developer evolved AI-co-developed code without AI, there was no significant difference in completion time [@borg2026echoes, p. 33], CodeHealth (8.49 vs 8.44) [@borg2026echoes, p. 38] or test coverage [@borg2026echoes, p. 35]. The only "significant" maintainability effect, a Bayesian +0.10 CodeHealth for code from habitual AI users, favours AI [@borg2026echoes, p. 39].
228	- **Differences**:
229	  - Data and population: real-world OSS repositories with ≥10 stars [@he2026speed, p. 4] vs one 2 KLoC Java/Spring Boot task done by 151 volunteer professionals [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @borg2026echoes, p. 64].
230	  - Tool generation: an agentic IDE (Cursor Composer/agent) [@he2026speed, p. 2] vs late-2024 assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) [@borg2026echoes, p. 3; @borg2026echoes, p. 60].
231	  - Metric: repository-total warnings and cognitive complexity, which scale with code size [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a LoC-weighted file-level CodeHealth average plus a second developer's evolution time [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
232	  - Time: monthly panel of up to about 20 months [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a single hand-off task.
233	  - Robustness: he2026speed's quality effects turn negative and non-significant under the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%) [@he2026speed, p. 16]. borg2026echoes is underpowered (75 of 128 planned participants; 80% power only for d≈0.66) [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
234	- **Partial agreement** [V]: borg2026echoes' observational Phase 1 also found more duplication (23% vs 11%), more complex conditionals and very large code-volume outliers in AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 30; @borg2026echoes, p. 46]. With size controlled, he2026speed finds no direct Cursor effect on warnings [@he2026speed, p. 8].
235	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two results need not conflict. Both fit "AI adds more code, and project-level totals rise with it, while per-file health and the short-term effort of the next developer are not clearly worse". The he2026speed effect depends on the estimator, and borg2026echoes can rule out only large effects. Neither study settles the question.
236	
237	### C2. Fewer or more static-analysis issues in LLM code? molison2025llm vs he2026speed
238	- **Side A** [V]: GPT-4o solutions had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged "bugs" than APPS human solutions (OR 0.00–0.019) [@molison2025llm, p. 8], and lower SonarQube fix effort on introductory and interview tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 7].
239	- **Side B** [V]: Cursor adoption raised repository SonarQube warnings by +30.26% [@he2026speed, p. 7].
240	- **Differences**:
241	  - Unit: per-solution odds of an issue in single-file stdin/stdout programs [@molison2025llm, p. 5] vs monthly repository totals [@he2026speed, p. 5].
242	  - Baseline: competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability [@molison2025llm, p. 9] vs matched non-adopting repositories, which may themselves use other AI tools [@he2026speed, p. 7].
243	  - Metric: the SonarQube "bug" category vs all reliability, maintainability and security warnings.
244	  - Leakage: molison2025llm's few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
245	  - Time: GPT-4o in 2024 vs Cursor agents in 2024–2025.
246	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the results are not comparable. Both use SonarQube, but the units, baselines and code types differ, so neither one refutes the other. molison2025llm's smell results are themselves mixed: zero-shot code had 3.57x the odds of a smell on introductory tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
247	
248	### C3. Which instrument measures the quality of AI code? zhu2026understanding vs SonarQube-based studies
249	- **Side A** [A]: zhu2026understanding chose PyExamine to separate structural and architectural smells from the "superficial linting issues" counted by SonarQube [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2; @zhu2026understanding, p. 4]. It found more Long Method smells in larger LLMs' code than in human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
250	- **Side B** [V]: SonarQube-based studies report fewer issues in LLM code [@molison2025llm, p. 8], a platform-dependent issue density (22.83 vs about 9 issues/KLOC) [@mota2026comparing, p. 5], or more warnings with adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7].
251	- **Context** [A]: technical-debt tools disagree on what counts as real debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5], and SonarQube and general linters were not designed for LLM-specific debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22]. mota2026comparing calls SonarQube an auxiliary indicator only [@mota2026comparing, p. 6]. borg2026echoes argues that CodeHealth outperforms the SonarQube Maintainability Rating; note that its first author works for CodeScene, the vendor of CodeHealth [@borg2026echoes, p. 4; @borg2026echoes, p. 75].
252	- **Differences**: the tools differ (PyExamine, SonarQube, CodeHealth, MI), and so do the task types (algorithmic snippets, generated web apps, OSS repositories). zhu2026understanding's Exp I counts are small, unnormalised and untested [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
253	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the direction of "LLM vs human code quality" may depend on the measuring instrument. The field has no validated, size-normalised maintainability measure for AI-generated code.
254	
255	### C4. Does iterative feedback or self-repair help? pan2026functional vs tran2026vibe / zhou2025declarui / wu2026looks
256	- **Side A** [V]: On GPT-5.2, three one-shot strategies all lowered the aggregate non-functional score without raising functional correctness: self-repair, environment repair and planning (NF 46.1–49.9% vs 57.1% at baseline) [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
257	- **Side B**:
258	  - [V] Browser self-testing during generation correlates with accuracy across 16 models (r = 0.72) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
259	  - [V] Removing DeclarUI's page-transition graph plus refinement loop cuts navigation coverage to 23.1% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10]. Its compile success is 98% vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9].
260	  - [V]/[A] A tsc + vite verify-repair loop gives 100% build success for all six models [@wu2026looks, p. 6]. The authors attribute this to the loop [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
261	- **Further evidence** [A]: agents' own validation missed behavioural mismatches with the reference [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
262	- **Differences**:
263	  - Feedback type: generic one-shot repair of a whole Python repository [@pan2026functional, p. 8], targeted compile and navigation checks [@zhou2025declarui, p. 5], and build checks [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
264	  - Design: a single-model intervention (pan2026functional) vs an observational correlation across models, where the system prompt itself demands browser testing [@tran2026vibe, p. 16].
265	  - Outcome: non-functional quality (pan2026functional) vs compilation, navigation or build (zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks).
266	  - Circularity: zhou2025declarui scores navigation against the same graph that guides its refinement [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
267	- **Possible explanation** [I]: feedback improves the property it checks (compilation, build, navigation edges). Self-testing goes along with stronger models. No study shows that generic repair improves both behavioural fidelity and code quality, and the only study that measures quality after repair finds harm (single model, single run).
268	
269	### C5. Do rebuilds "look right but behave wrong"? chen2025iwr / lu2025webgen / xiao2025benchmarking vs bai2026recreationworld / wu2026looks
270	- **Side A** [V]:
271	  - Interactive functionality is below visual fidelity for all 28 models (GPT-5 IFS 24.39 vs VFS 64.25) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
272	  - Design-validation tests are passed more often than functional tests (e.g. 44.3% vs 21.1%) [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
273	  - Interactive regions score lower than full pages for all six models [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
274	- **Side B** [V]:
275	  - In bai2026recreationworld the visual (VLM) channel is below the programmatic channel for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11], although static structure beats actions within the programmatic tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
276	  - In wu2026looks navigation passes 58–92% [@wu2026looks, p. 7], while visual fidelity stays at or below 2.99/5 [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
277	- **Differences**:
278	  - chen2025iwr's VFS is averaged only over reached checkpoints, so part of its IFS<VFS gap comes from how the metrics are built [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
279	  - Visual scores come from different instruments: OCR+DINO+MLLM rubric, VLM assertions, Borda ranks and CLIP.
280	  - Functional scores also differ: action replay, accessibility tests and navigation tests.
281	- **Possible explanation** [I]: bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr are only *directionally consistent* on one point: static structure is reproduced more easily than interaction logic. The broader claim "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity" is not supported, because the visual and functional scales are not commensurable across or within papers.
282	
283	### C6. Multi-agent / agentic frameworks: MetaGPT fails in liu2026benchmarking but leads in mock2026vibe
284	- **Side A** [V]: MetaGPT nearly always fails on E2EDev (0–5.4% Req.Acc) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6]. Multi-agent frameworks "do not consistently improve" over a plain LLM (by our count, 9 of 24 cells higher [I]) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
285	- **Side B** [V]: Agentic MetaGPT X runs had the highest test pass rate (mean 94.58%) [@mock2026vibe, p. 25; @mock2026vibe, p. 41]. zhu2026understanding generated complete multi-file apps with MetaGPT, but only after adding explicit modularity prompts [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
286	- **Differences**:
287	  - Task size: a two-function string task [@mock2026vibe, p. 12] vs 46 multi-requirement web apps.
288	  - Backbone: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] vs older or smaller backbones such as GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
289	  - Product: MetaGPT X web interface vs the open-source framework.
290	  - Evaluation: 12 runs pooled vs 46 projects x 3 runs.
291	- **Possible explanation** [I]: framework value depends on the backbone and the task scale. mock2026vibe's agentic advantage is confounded with the newer model generation.
292	
293	### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe
294	- **Side A** [V]: Reference-normalised security averages 87.40% and is the strongest non-functional dimension [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
295	- **Side B** [V]: 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best agent fail targeted security tests, and SecPass is only 3.8–12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
296	- **Differences**: pan2026functional counts high-risk static findings relative to the reference, and the score can reward incomplete code. zhao2025vibe runs 3.5 targeted security tests per task for a known historical CWE [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. The tasks also differ: whole-repository generation vs security-sensitive feature patches.
297	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two instruments measure different things, a static absence of flagged patterns vs exploit-relevant behaviour. "Secure" cannot be compared across them.
298	
299	### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
300	- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. In bai2026recreationworld they are 89.4% smaller with 92.3% fewer files (4 of 10 models; desktop and Android only) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. In yang2026programbench they are shorter (median 1,173 vs 3,068 lines) and use fewer files [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
301	- **Side B** [V]:
302	  - Cursor adoption raises lines added by +281.3% in month 1 [@he2026speed, p. 8].
303	  - AI-assisted Task 1 code produced outliers of up to 10,788 lines [@borg2026echoes, p. 30].
304	  - In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts track code size (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
305	  - The visual-fidelity leader writes 1,441 LoC vs 668 for GPT-5 [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
306	- **Differences**: rebuilds from scratch scored against a behavioural oracle of a mature original, vs incremental additions to existing projects or apps generated from a spec.
307	- **Possible explanation** [I]: reconstructions under-implement the original, which is consistent with low full-pass rates. Assisted development adds volume. Size therefore carries opposite signals in the two settings, and size-driven quality metrics (smell counts, totals) must be normalised before comparison.
308	
309	### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)
310	- **"Vibe coding" means different things** [V]:
311	  - fawzy2026vibe: natural-language prompting plus re-prompting with minimal review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
312	  - asdaque2026novice: a supervised agent workflow, operationalised as opening agentic PRs [@asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. Its authors warn that the findings may not hold under a broader definition [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4].
313	  - mock2026vibe: human-written TDD tests plus scripted prompts that participants could not modify [@mock2026vibe, p. 15].
314	  - he2026speed: Cursor configuration files committed to a repository (intent-to-treat) [@he2026speed, p. 4].
315	  - ehsani2026faster: a driver of fast-integration debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 17].
316	  - [I] These are different interventions. Their results should not be pooled as "effects of vibe coding".
317	- **Fidelity scores are not comparable** [V]:
318	  - 58.06% average of programmatic and VLM channels [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
319	  - 36.35 Final Score (0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
320	  - 49.15% cumulative workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
321	  - 53.75% Req.Acc with `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
322	  - 27.8% UI-agent accuracy with half credit for PARTIAL [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
323	  - 61.77% workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 6].
324	  - 0% resolved / 3% almost [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
325	  - [I] Each figure uses a different oracle, input, application type and model generation. Do not rank across them.
326	
327	### C10. Same model family builds or judges the benchmark and is evaluated (possible bias; untested)
328	- **Overlap and the same family wins** [V]:
329	  - yang2026programbench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 wrote the tests [@yang2026programbench, p. 3], and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 31].
330	  - tran2026vibe: GPT-5 drafted the specs [@tran2026vibe, p. 3], and GPT-5.3-Codex ranks first [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]. The canonical judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5 [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
331	  - kim2026programdistill: GPT-5.6 Sol builds the tasks [@kim2026programdistill, p. 2], GPT-6 Astra ranks first [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8], and GPT-6 Astra also classifies the failures [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
332	  - zhao2025vibe: Claude 4 Sonnet runs the environment-building agent [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17], and SWE-agent constructs the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. The best setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
333	- **Overlap without a visible advantage** [V]:
334	  - liu2026benchmarking: GPT-4o built the annotations and is evaluated [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 13]; the best backbone is Claude-Haiku.
335	  - lu2025webgen: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and scored low [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
336	  - bai2026recreationworld: the Qwen3.7-Plus judge is the lowest-scoring model (average 9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
337	  - chen2025iwr: the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge ranks mid-table [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
338	  - wu2026looks: the judge is Gemini 2.5 Pro, Opus leads [@wu2026looks, p. 13], and the authors report no self-preference [A].
339	- [I] No paper tests construction-model or judge-model self-preference directly. The pattern is a validity threat, not a demonstrated bias.
340	
341	## Agreements / converging evidence
342	
343	- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
344	  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
345	  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
346	  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
347	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
348	- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
349	  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
350	  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
351	  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
352	  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
353	  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
354	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
355	- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
356	- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
357	  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
358	  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
359	  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
360	  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
361	  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
362	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
363	- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
364	- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
365	  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
366	  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
367	  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
368	  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
369	- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
